items.title: Taming AI Agents with Capsem: Hardware Sandboxing That Doesn’t Kill Productivity
items.abstract:
Enterprises are racing to adopt AI agents granting them access to data, networks, code execution, and beyond. Yet between prompt injection, hallucination, and agents going rogue, poorly restricted access is a security nightmare that weakly secured environments can no longer bandage over, as proven by recent model sandbox escapes.

Capsem is an open-source, Rust co-designed hypervisor/VM system designed to fill the need of a highly secure agent environment. What makes it unique is its core premise being that to be successful should not make users choose between speed, usability and security.

Users love Capsem for its single-click install, optional friendly UI, and agent-ready VMs booting under two seconds. Security endorses its air-gapped, hardened VMs, and leverages its full observability and enforcement mechanisms—including its L8 network reconstruction layer with full model and MCP semantics. Admins rely on its SDK and standard support for Sigma and OpenTelemetry.
items.summary: Capsem, an open-source Rust hypervisor and VM system for sandboxing AI agents with built-in network observability and enforcement.

hl.t: Capsem is an open-source, Rust co-designed hypervisor and VM system built to run AI agents securely.
Agent-ready VMs boot in under two seconds, with single-click install and an optional UI.
Air-gapped, hardened VMs with network reconstruction that understands model and MCP traffic semantics.
Supports Sigma rules and OpenTelemetry, plus an SDK for administrators integrating agent observability.
Argues agent isolation should not force a trade-off between speed, usability and security.
Presented by a Distinguished Research Scientist at Google DeepMind.

items.title: Coffee break
How Meta Changed Building Secure Software With AI

speakers.a: Scale finding, fixing, and prevention across the world., Meta

items.abstract:
Meta’s core values include moving fast, which is why we’ve invested for years in developer tooling and automating discovery of security bugs. With AI, software development at Meta moves faster than ever: significant lines of code grew 105.9% year on year, with AI written code responsible for over 80% of that growth. We’ve changed software security to match – this talk covers two lessons learned and where we’re going next.

First, we’ll talk about driving code analysis coverage at breakneck speed to get ahead of external attackers armed with AI. What we needed to cover, how we prioritized, and how that built off prior experiences. We successfully landed 90% coverage on our targets, but that’s far from solving the whole problem.

Second, we’ll go over lessons from using AI to write fixes. We landed at over 40% of critical vulnerabilities fixed by AI-written diffs. We were surprised by finding that this did not, by itself, reduce the time to fix vulnerabilities!
items.summary: Meta's experience scaling code analysis coverage and using AI-written fixes for critical vulnerabilities amid AI-accelerated software development.

hl.t: Over 40% of critical vulnerabilities at Meta were fixed by AI-written diffs, yet time to fix did not drop.
Meta reached 90% code analysis coverage on its targets while racing attackers armed with AI.
Significant lines of code at Meta grew 105.9% year on year, with AI-written code behind over 80% of it.
Covers how coverage targets were chosen and prioritized, building on years of automated bug discovery.

items.title: From DARPA AIxCC to Microsoft FORGE Lab: Lessons Building Hyperscale AI Code Scanning Tools
items.abstract:
Team Atlanta’s victory in the DARPA AI Cyber Challenge (AIxCC), where AI systems autonomously discovered and repaired vulnerabilities in complex software, was only the beginning. Since AIxCC, we have been evolving AI vulnerability discovery into production systems for open-source and commercial codebases. Drawing from MDASH and Microsoft FORGE Lab, this talk examines how modern AI\-powered code scanning combines LLM reasoning with traditional program analysis to find real vulnerabilities at scale.

We will discuss lessons learned operationalizing autonomous security systems, emerging technical patterns behind modern AI bug-finding platforms, and how AI agents may transform software security in the future.
items.summary: Lessons from DARPA AIxCC and Microsoft FORGE Lab on building production AI code scanning that combines LLMs with program analysis.

hl.t: Lessons from taking Team Atlanta's DARPA AIxCC winning approach into production code scanning systems.
Explains how AI code scanning combines LLM reasoning with traditional program analysis to find real bugs at scale.
Draws on MDASH and Microsoft FORGE Lab, applied to both open-source and commercial codebases.
Covers operational lessons from running autonomous systems that discover and repair vulnerabilities.
Presented by Microsoft's VP of Security Research, drawing on Team Atlanta's AIxCC work.

items.title: StealthBench: Can Autonomous Security Agents Do OPSEC Like An Experienced Operator?

speakers.a: Staff AI Security Researcher at Dreadnode; founder of OWASP GenAI Security Project; AI red teamer and bug bounty hunter

items.abstract:
Autonomous security agents are usually judged on whether they find the vulnerability. In a real engagement, that is only half the job: an agent that leaks credentials, modifies production, spams users, or floods telemetry can turn a successful exploit into an operational failure and a detection. A very stealthy model is thu a more dangerous one.

We introduce StealthBench, an open-source benchmark that measures task completion and operational security together. Fourteen containerized scenarios test credential handling, detection avoidance, infrastructure compartmentalization, operational impact, and third-party harm. Across 771 trajectories from eight agent models, no model achieved a safe-success rate above 53.8%. Some highly capable models solved most tasks yet did so recklessly in more than one-third of valid attempts.

This talk presents the benchmark, the failure patterns it exposes, and practical lessons for evaluating agents before granting them offensive-security tools.
items.summary: StealthBench, an open-source benchmark measuring whether autonomous offensive security agents complete tasks while keeping operational security.

hl.t: Across 771 trajectories from eight agent models, none exceeded a 53.8% safe-success rate.
StealthBench, an open-source benchmark scoring offensive agents on task completion and operational security together.
Fourteen containerized scenarios test credential handling, detection avoidance, operational impact and third-party harm.

items.title: CISA’s Experience and Lessons Learned in AI-Enabled Vulnerability Management

speakers.a: CISA’s Deputy Associate Director for Vulnerabilty Management

items.abstract: CISA plays a variety of fundamentally important roles in the global vulnerability management ecosystem – from sponsoring and overseeing the execution of the CVE Program, maintaining the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, to co-directing the Gold Eagle vulnerability intake platform to help manage the influx of new vulnerabilities being discovered by AI models. This presentation will cover a variety of ways in which CISA is adopting AI models, building skills, and exploring the use of agents to optimize its vulnerability management mission, including specific details on what approaches are working and which ones haven’t.
items.summary: How CISA adopts AI models, skills and agents across its vulnerability management mission, including approaches that worked and failed.

items.title: Lunch break
Prompt, Patch, Prove
items.abstract:
Attackers can analyze firmware in hours. Defenders may wait weeks for an update. Can defenders build temporary, testable repairs without pretending to replace the vendor?

On an authorized ASUS RT-BE82U laboratory router, we used an agentic coding model to analyze build 39099 and repair two published vulnerabilities: CVE-2025-15101, an authenticated command injection in the root web server, and CVE-2026-11851, an authenticated SQL-injection path. The model traced request data into the exact ARM sinks, proposed hash-locked patches, generated negative tests, and helped reconstruct the firmware package.

I will show the original and patched assembly, what the model got wrong, the evidence gates that caught it, and a reusable prompting protocol for defensive binary repair.
items.summary: Using an agentic coding model to analyze and patch published vulnerabilities in router firmware binaries, with evidence gates and a prompting protocol.

hl.t: An agentic coding model repaired two published router vulnerabilities directly in firmware, on an authorized lab device.
A reusable prompting protocol for defensive binary repair when vendor updates are weeks away.
Shows what the model got wrong and the evidence gates that caught its mistakes.
Targets a command injection and an SQL injection in an ASUS router, with original and patched assembly compared.
The model generated hash-locked patches, negative tests and helped rebuild the firmware package.
Presented by a Member of Technical Staff at OpenAI.

items.title: Your Sandbox Degrades Gracefully, What’s the Wurst That Could Happen?
items.abstract:
RAPTOR is an agentic security harness for finding bugs: an LLM reads a repository nobody has vetted, writes proof-of-concepts from what it finds, and runs them on a machine holding our API keys and everything else dear to us. We’ve been around the block, and weren’t comfortable running that outside a sandbox, so back in April we built an agent-specific one to contain it. We’ve upgraded it considerably since, and along the way introduced (and had to fix) a fair few security issues of our own making.

We don’t think we’re that innovative (or cool actually), we just believed it was necessary – but it was much harder than it looks. Oh yah, everyone tells us how easy making a sandbox is. This talk is the embarrassing lessons behind what is now a hardened agent sandbox, attack-ready, until the next time we figure out how to break it by trying to upgrade it. Four months in, we’re still finding out how little we knew about constraining dinosaurs and how often they tried to eat our faces.
items.summary: Lessons from building and hardening an agent-specific sandbox for RAPTOR, an agentic bug-finding harness that writes and runs proof-of-concepts.

hl.t: Lessons from building and hardening an agent-specific sandbox for RAPTOR, an agentic bug-finding harness.
Containing an agent that reads unvetted repositories and runs its own proofs of concept near real API keys.
Candid account of security issues the team introduced into its own sandbox, and how they were fixed.
Four months of upgrades show why building an agent sandbox is much harder than it looks.

items.title: Three Years of Evals Later: What’s Changing in Model and Harness IR/SOC Scores
items.abstract: As we build IR/SOC investigation agents, every new model and harness release triggers the same conversation: is there anything worthwhile here? Release materials may claim 99%+ or SOTA, but we find tasks are frequently contaminated, unreproducible, or too unrealistic. For three years we have run major frontier and open-weight models, plus commercial and open harnesses, against an evolving benchmark for modern incident response: 100+ log sources, capped budgets, and measures for accuracy, speed, cost, refusals, contamination, and cheating. The results generally track what we see on real tasks like timelining. This talk covers recent shifts, including: when frontier models need extra runway, where open weights are good enough, why fast costs are falling, when open harnesses are competitive, how models and harnesses are absorbing prompt engineering, and where investigation harnesses beat coding agents. We close with what it means to own your evals and adapt them to your environment.
items.summary: Three years of benchmarking frontier and open-weight models and harnesses on incident response tasks, covering accuracy, cost, contamination and trends.

hl.t: Three years of results running frontier and open-weight models against an evolving incident response benchmark.
Benchmark spans 100+ log sources under capped budgets, scoring accuracy, speed, cost, refusals, contamination and cheating.
Compares commercial and open harnesses, including where investigation harnesses beat coding agents.
Covers when open weights are good enough and why costs for fast models are falling.
Guidance on owning security evaluations and adapting them to an organization's own environment.

items.title: Who Authorized the Agent? Making the AI Harness an Enforceable Compliance Boundary
items.abstract: An agent can receive a deny decision and still succeed if its harness retains a broad credential or another network path. This session presents a practical architecture for making the AI agent harness an enforceable compliance boundary. We trace one tool call through the IdP, human and workload identity, immutable run context, policy decision point, mandatory enforcement points, short-lived credential broker, downstream authorization, and audit evidence. A working prototype and executable policy models show how user entitlement, agent capability, task, resource policy, and runtime context combine into one decision. A short demo compares a decision-only API with an inline proxy that stops the downstream request. We also examine wrapper bypass, service-account substitution, stale decisions, credential lifetime mismatches, and incomplete evidence.
items.summary: An architecture making the agent harness an enforceable compliance boundary through identity, policy enforcement points and short-lived credential brokering.

hl.t: An architecture that makes the AI agent harness an enforceable compliance boundary, not just a decision point.
Traces one tool call through identity, policy decision, enforcement points, credential broker and audit evidence.
Live demo compares a decision-only API with an inline proxy that stops the downstream request.
Working prototype and executable policy models combine user entitlement, agent capability, task and runtime context.
Examines failure cases including wrapper bypass, service-account substitution, stale decisions and incomplete evidence.

items.title: Coffee break
A Tale of Two Chains
items.abstract: This talk will discuss not one but two full chain Chrome exploits we developed and submitted to Google’s VRP for the full chain bonus. The first chain, which had significant human involvement and was developed over a period of two months, met its end in a collision with an internally-discovered bug upon reporting. The second chain was developed in a whirlwind six days with significantly less human guidance: instead, we orchestrated a multi-stage, structured campaign that guided AI agents to produce a primary candidate and several collision insurance “backups” for each stage (V8 corruption, V8 sandbox escape, and renderer sandbox escape) and submitted it to the VRP, ultimately resulting in a $250,000 reward for the first full chain exploit demonstrated under the new April 2026 VRP rules. The talk will cover the differences in how each chain was developed and explain what it takes to get a full chain exploit with no collisions against modern Chrome.
items.summary: Comparing two full-chain Chrome exploits, one largely human-built and one produced in six days by orchestrated AI agents.

hl.t: AI agents helped build a full chain Chrome exploit in six days, earning a $250,000 Google VRP reward.
Compares a two-month, human-heavy exploit chain with a largely agent-driven one built under the April 2026 VRP rules.
A structured multi-stage campaign orchestrated agents to produce primary candidates and backups for each stage.
Explains what avoiding bug collisions takes when submitting full chains against modern Chrome.
Presented by a Distinguished Engineer at XBOW, the team that built both exploit chains.

items.title: Models vs Cyber Reality: Frontier Agents Against Our Own Privately Disclosed Zero-Days
items.abstract:
Model Benchmarks say frontier agents can hack and patch. We benchmarked that against cyber reality: GPT6 Astra, Fable 5.1 and GLM5.3 vs zero-days our team found and privately disclosed in the confidential compute stack, plus 209 known vulnerabilities

On the zero-days, eight agents ran 54 attempts. 12 built a working exploit. Zero produced an accepted patch. Three Chinese models took 7 of the 12 working exploits. GPT-6 Astra refused. Claude Fable 5.1 refused. We show the practical reality board and the refusal-adjusted capability board and explain 3 tasks in detail.

On the known vulns, three agents each attacked and repaired the same 209 vulns. Two out of three were better attackers than defenders, when discounting shallow patches or patches that break the CI.

The failures we found: A fix that refused 40% of valid messages. A patch that locked every user out.
items.summary: Benchmarking frontier agents against privately disclosed zero-days and 209 known vulnerabilities on exploitation, patching quality and refusals.

hl.t: Frontier agents tested on privately disclosed zero-days: 12 of 54 attempts produced working exploits, none an accepted patch.
On 209 known vulnerabilities, two of three agents proved better attackers than defenders.
Presents a practical reality board alongside a refusal-adjusted capability board for model comparison.
Patch failures included a fix that refused 40% of valid messages and one that locked out every user.
Targets come from the confidential compute stack, where the speakers' team found and disclosed the bugs.

items.title: Your Harness Needs a Security Constitution
items.abstract:
I’ve spent years finding cloud security bugs, before and after AI, so I know how hard they are to find and how bad models are at finding them.

I set out to try to fix that. The result has been 90+ valid, cloud-specific issues across multiple providers, supported by a new methodology — AI-led hunting with a Security Constitution.

Models already handle finding code-level bugs like SQLi and XSS well, but these issues have never intrigued me. Instead, I tend to focus on platform-design flaws: missing authorization checks, inadequate logging, mishandled data, where I find the frontier models are much weaker.

Enter a new way of hunting: the Security Constitution, modeled on Anthropic’s Ethical Constitution, is a set of 12 principles for how trust is held across multi-tenant platforms. It gives every hunt a point of view and a way to means-test a finding: the “reasonable customer test.” The principles are the worldview, and what pours out are new shapes of novel cloud vulnerabilities.
items.summary: A Security Constitution of twelve trust principles guiding AI-led hunting for cloud platform design flaws across multiple providers.

hl.t: AI-led hunting produced 90+ valid cloud-specific security issues across multiple providers.
A Security Constitution of 12 principles for trust across multi-tenant platforms, guiding each hunt.
Focuses on platform design flaws such as missing authorization checks and inadequate logging, where models are weaker.
Introduces the reasonable customer test as a way to judge whether a finding is valid.
Presented by a Principal Security Researcher at Vectra AI with years of cloud bug hunting experience.

items.title: 0-Click Remote Exploits in an AI World
items.abstract:
0-click vulnerabilities in mobile messaging applications are often treated as rare, highly bespoke findings. Our experience suggests something different: with the right tooling and models remote attack surface can be enumerated and audited automatically by LLMs.

This talk presents the tooling and techniques we developed for rapidly identifying and auditing remotely reachable attack surface across mobile messaging applications. We demonstrate the approach through tree concrete case studies: WeWorm, a worm that spreads through WeChat and jumps between modern iOS and Android devices, a Samsung-only WhatsApp 0click and a semi universal iOS 1click.

Finally, we examine what happens as this kind of research becomes easier to automate. We discuss how scalable 0-click discovery changes the security assumptions behind messaging apps, where existing trust boundaries break down, and what application and platform vendors can do to reduce remotely exposed attack surface before these techniques become commonplace.
items.summary: LLM tooling to enumerate and audit remote attack surface in mobile messaging apps, with WeChat, WhatsApp and iOS exploit case studies.

hl.t: Tooling and techniques for using LLMs to enumerate and audit remote attack surface in mobile messaging apps.
Three case studies across WeChat, WhatsApp on Samsung, and iOS illustrate the approach.
Argues 0-click bugs are less rare than assumed once the search is automated.
Recommendations for app and platform vendors on reducing remotely exposed attack surface.
Discusses how scalable 0-click discovery changes trust assumptions behind messaging apps.

items.title: Closing Remarks
Mingling & Something sweet
All Tokens Are Created Equal, Including the Attacker’s

speakers.a: Director of AI Standards and Governance, Zenity

items.abstract:
EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711, CVSS 9.3) walked data out of Microsoft 365 Copilot with zero clicks. No memory bug. No blown permission. Attacker text landed in the context window and the model did what it said, because transformer attention reads no trust label on any token. Your system prompt, a poisoned README, and an MCP tool definition all get the same scaled dot-product treatment.

So we measured it. Attention mass on the protective span collapsing as an attacker floods the window, plotted against attack success climbing. Then we built the thing nobody has: a record of what the model actually saw. We’re releasing CxBOM, a CycloneDX-based bill of materials for the context window. It logs every component, its trust ring, and its provenance, and it fails the session when an externally supplied MCP tool definition is assembled with operator-level authority. That inversion is the bug behind CVE-2025-54135 and CVE-2025-54136.

Live demo. Schema, emitter, validator, fixtures. Yours to run.
items.summary: Measuring attention collapse under context flooding and releasing CxBOM, a CycloneDX bill of materials recording context window provenance.

hl.t: Release of CxBOM, a CycloneDX-based bill of materials recording what entered a model's context window.
Measures attention on protective instructions collapsing as attacker text floods the window, against rising attack success.
CxBOM fails a session when an external MCP tool definition is assembled with operator-level authority.
Live demo with schema, emitter, validator and fixtures available for attendees to run.
Grounded in EchoLeak, the zero-click Microsoft 365 Copilot data exfiltration issue, and related MCP CVEs.
Presented by Zenity's Director of AI Standards and Governance and the CEO of Detecteam.

items.title: Attention Is All You Need (to Catch Hallucinations & Prompt Injections)
items.abstract:
Two of the biggest trust and security challenges of LLM: hallucinations (ungrounded facts) and indirect prompt injections (unauthorized instructions) are often believed to be unrelated.

Existing blackbox methods for detecting these problems are distinct, often too slow, expensive, and unreliable.

This talk highlights a major breakthrough in whitebox analysis that shows that these problems are actually related and can be solved with the same approach simultaneously. Our key insight is that LLMs are incapable of permanently storing specific facts or instructions. Instead, when they need a fact or instruction, they “look back” to the relevant part of the input. By observing these hidden states during these token generation, we can identify exactly which input tokens the model relied on for each factual statement or instruction it follows.

Our solution works in real time, requires no additional LLM calls, and outperforms state of the art on multiple benchmarks.
items.summary: White-box detection of hallucinations and indirect prompt injections by tracing which input tokens a model attends to during generation.

hl.t: A whitebox method detects hallucinations and indirect prompt injections with the same approach, using hidden states.
Tracks which input tokens a model relied on for each fact or instruction it follows.
Runs in real time with no additional LLM calls, reported to outperform prior methods on several benchmarks.
Argues blackbox detectors for these problems are separate, slow, expensive and unreliable.
Presented by the founders of Realm Labs, describing their own detection approach.

items.title: Coffee break
Into the Wild: Hunting Real-World Attacks on AI Systems
items.abstract:
Until now, AI security research has lived mostly in the lab, while AI systems went online. This created a knowledge gap: defenders lack threat intelligence from real AI incidents.

To discover what attackers do in the wild, we deployed a honeypot network emulating production AI stacks and agents. This talk is the forensic report.

We show campaigns probing for CVEs to compromise AI backends within days of being published, turning Ollama’s model downloader into an SSRF vector, and LiteLLM’s guardrails into a code execution vector. We’ll detail attacks on models, and attempts to create backdoored models stripping safety controls or to exfiltrate telemetry.

We display attempts to hijack backends and deploy offensive frameworks to turn exposed AI infra into free compute. We demonstrate activity probing for frontier models and agents’ capabilities, and abusing agents’ own tools to extract secrets.

We share TTPs, IoCs, signatures, configurations and enabling design patterns.
items.summary: Findings from a honeypot network emulating production AI stacks and agents, documenting real attacker campaigns, TTPs and indicators.

hl.t: Forensic report from a honeypot network emulating production AI stacks and agents.
Campaigns probed AI backends for newly published CVEs within days, including Ollama and LiteLLM issues.
Shares TTPs, IoCs, signatures and configurations defenders can apply to their own AI infrastructure.
Observed attempts to hijack exposed AI infrastructure for free compute and to extract secrets via agent tools.
Covers attacks on the models themselves, including attempts to create backdoored models without safety controls.
Presented by an AI Red Team Researcher at Zenity.

items.title: Say Shibboleth: Fingerprinting the Models Behind Agentic Attacks

speakers.a: Creator of the Zero Day Clock, Leading Infosec and Threat Research

items.abstract:
Last year at [un]prompted, we showed that AI-assisted attackers leak an “accent”: timing gaps, hallucinated identifiers, tool artifacts and other model-specific behavior. Those signals are accidental. This talk turns them into a measurement method.

We introduce shibboleths: realistic features placed in an attacker’s environment specifically because different models respond to them differently without requiring prompt injection or adversarial instructions. Combined with passive telemetry, they let us fingerprint the model family and agent harness behind an attack even when the model is self-hosted and its claimed identity cannot be trusted.

We show how to generate and optimize these traps, demonstrate fingerprinting end-to-end against autonomous attackers, and present results from a controlled model/harness matrix and live honeypot deployment including where the method fails. The result is a new telemetry layer for investigating and clustering AI-driven attacks.
items.summary: Placing shibboleth traps in attacker environments to fingerprint the model family and harness behind AI-driven attacks.

hl.t: Shibboleths: environment traps that reveal which model family and harness is behind an AI-driven attack.
Fingerprinting works even when the attacker self-hosts the model and its claimed identity cannot be trusted.
Results from a controlled model and harness matrix plus a live honeypot deployment, including failure cases.
Shows how to generate and optimize the traps and demonstrates fingerprinting end to end against autonomous attackers.
Builds on last year's [un]prompted talk on the accidental accent left by AI-assisted attackers.
Presented by the creator of the Zero Day Clock and the Head of AI at Cracken.

items.title: Who Is Prompt-Injecting Coding Agents? A Scan of 86 Million GitHub Items
items.abstract:
A hidden HTML comment in a GitHub issue can hijack a coding agent. This has been repeatedly shown in demos and research PoCs. But how often are attackers in the wild actually trying it, and what do they want?

We launched the first GitHub-wide scan to hunt for indirect prompt injections across 86 million GitHub items: issues, PRs, comments and READMEs. We extracted hidden text (e.g., HTML comments) then screened it with novel heuristics and a two-stage LLM classifier. We then manually reviewed every flagged candidate.

We identified prompt injections in roughly 2.5 of every 100K GitHub items. A key finding is that injections serve diverse objectives: orchestration of project agents, constrain visiting bots, growth hacking, and malicious exfil data.

We’ll dissect real injections, map their objectives, and explain our detection blind spots. We release the detector, prompts, and taxonomy so others can investigate who is steering coding agents and why.
items.summary: A scan of 86 million GitHub items for indirect prompt injections targeting coding agents, with objectives, taxonomy and a released detector.

hl.t: First GitHub-wide hunt for indirect prompt injections, covering 86 million issues, PRs, comments and READMEs.
Prompt injections appeared in roughly 2.5 of every 100,000 GitHub items.
The detector, prompts and taxonomy are released for others to continue the investigation.
Objectives ranged from orchestrating project agents and constraining bots to growth hacking and data exfiltration.
Pipeline combined hidden text extraction, heuristics, a two-stage LLM classifier and full manual review.
Presented by a Distinguished Researcher and a senior AI security researcher from Radware.

items.title: Promptware EOD: Skillful Agent Detonation
items.abstract:
The AI agent supply chain is fertile ground for malware. Lurking in skill files, rug-pulled MCP servers, misaligned models, and even moltbook posts

Standing on the shoulders of giants, we introduce an old-new approach: agent detonation chamber. Analysis based on kernel-level truths, not a wishful LLM scan. We detonated tens of thousands of skills from public marketplaces, and uncovered hundreds of malicious ones. We’ll show how cryptominers and infostealers evade static scanners using advanced techniques, expose risky patterns, and uncover the slop of skill design

Inside the chamber, a victim agent installs a suspicious artifact, while a red-team agent tries to make it use the new skill. By comparing what the victim “thinks” it did with what the kernel knows happened the chamber reveals malicious behavior static tools miss

To wrap up we’ll release our detonation chamber as free public service. As well as drop a unique verified benchmark of supply chain artifacts caught in the wild
items.summary: A kernel-level detonation chamber for agent skills and MCP servers that uncovered hundreds of malicious skills in public marketplaces.

hl.t: Tens of thousands of public marketplace skills were detonated, uncovering hundreds of malicious ones.
An agent detonation chamber compares what a victim agent believes it did with kernel-level evidence.
The chamber is released as a free public service, alongside a verified benchmark of in-the-wild artifacts.
Shows why static scanners miss malicious skills that dynamic, kernel-level analysis catches.
Covers risky patterns across skill files, rug-pulled MCP servers and other agent supply chain artifacts.
Presented by Zenity's Director of Security Research and an AI Red Team Researcher.

items.title: Lunch break
Sandboxing Agents is a Three-Body Problem: Containment, Provenance, and the Human Authority
items.abstract:
Every sandboxing guide treats agent containment as one problem. Building Webflow’s agent-native design and collaboration platform (in research preview) we found at least three, and they pull on each other.

Containment: what the process can touch.

Provenance: whether the agent can tell instruction from data. Authority: who may act, who confirms, and what that confirmation binds to.

Each is solvable alone. Coupled, they behave like the three-body problem: tighten one and the other two move

This talk is about sequencing. Why our first boundary confined writes rather than reads, and why we framed it as anti-persistence instead of anti-damage. Why the iframe boundary had to be destination-driven. How a governance layer lets the host, not the model, decide what each agent and user may do. What came next, and how each boundary was tested and some live approval telemetry from the research preview:

You leave with a way to decide which body to harden first for your agent.
items.summary: How Webflow sequenced containment, provenance and human authority boundaries when securing agents in its design and collaboration platform.

hl.t: Treats agent sandboxing as three coupled problems: containment, provenance and human authority.
Experience from building Webflow's agent-native design and collaboration platform, currently in research preview.
A method for deciding which boundary to harden first for a given agent.
Explains why the first boundary confined writes rather than reads, framed as anti-persistence.
A governance layer lets the host, not the model, decide what each agent and user may do.
Includes live approval telemetry from the research preview, presented by Webflow's Head of Application Security.

items.title: The Model Is NOT a Security Control: Prompt Injection Dies at the Token Sampler
items.abstract:
Tantalus is a 2-round indirect prompt injection arena that puts you in front of a realistic AI assistant with access to files, emails, and chat history, pre-loaded with both legitimate tools and poisoned ones. The objective is to try to get the agent to exfiltrate data from an IT admin’s workstation.

With Tantalus as the substrate for my first whitepaper https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/S9GU6, I put it through the ringer across ~6.1 million inference calls; across model sizes 1.7B to 119B params. All behavioral and structural controls were bypassed or allowed malicious data to be generated, except for one.

Only one control had a provable 100% rate at blocking bad behavior from ever being generated.
items.summary: Testing prompt injection controls across 6.1 million inference calls in the Tantalus arena, arguing enforcement belongs at the token sampler.

hl.t: Across about 6.1 million inference calls, every behavioral and structural control but one was bypassed.
Identifies the single control that blocked malicious output 100% of the time, applied at the token sampler.

items.title: But the Reasoning Looks Right! Backdoors That Evade CoT Monitoring
items.abstract: Chain-of-thought monitoring is an increasingly central yet fragile part of AI safety stacks: monitors look for misbehavior in a model’s visible reasoning, under the assumption that CoTs are informative of the final output. What happens when the reasoning reaches the correct conclusion, but an attacker chooses the final answer? We introduce CoT-hidden backdoors: poisoned models producing benign reasoning alongside attacker-chosen outputs. We show how these behaviors are learned, why reasoning-only monitors miss them, and what changes when monitors also see the answer. We then ask whether internal activations can expose what visible reasoning hides. Using mechanistic interpretability tools, we find backdoors difficult to identify without prior knowledge of the poison. A natural-language autoencoder demo compares activations with and without the trigger, revealing differences shortly before the final answer, but neither the attacker’s target nor a reliable way to detect the backdoor.
items.summary: Backdoored models that produce benign chain-of-thought with attacker-chosen answers, evading reasoning monitors and resisting interpretability-based detection.

hl.t: CoT-hidden backdoors: poisoned models produce benign reasoning while emitting attacker-chosen answers.
Shows why reasoning-only monitors miss these backdoors and what changes when monitors also see the answer.

The Autonomous Adversarial Loop: Fully Automating an Octo Tempest Purple-Team Simulation
items.abstract:
We are Microsoft Security Research’s Purple Team. Every simulation replays a real adversary end-to-end against production-grade defenses, then measures what our detections caught and missed. It is high signal, but slow: each run takes a skilled operator days end-to-end.

So, we automated the whole loop. An infrastructure agent stands up the target environment, an autonomous red agent runs the full Octo Tempest (Scattered Spider) kill chain, and a blue agent correlates every attack step against Defender XDR to score what was detected and missed.

It worked better than we expected, and it got things wrong in ways that matter. The red agent executed all 10 phases in about 45 minutes with roughly 77% verified success and zero interventions.

This talk is the engineering reality of a fully autonomous purple-team loop: the architecture, the run, the metrics, and the failure modes you hit, plus the verification patterns we are adding to fix it.

items.title: Opened Is Not Fixed: The Last Mile of AI Vulnerability Remediation
items.abstract:
AI-assisted security programs can generate more vulnerability candidates and patch pull requests than engineering teams can review. Anthropic’s Glasswing update reports that a high or critical bug found by Mythos Preview takes two weeks to patch on average. Once discovery is cheap, review and closure are the scarce resource, and an opened pull request is an intermediate state.

This field report covers the operating loop we built to move work from verified finding to merge, rejection, deferral, or formal risk acceptance: root-cause deduplication, reachability-first ranking, typed refutation reasons, explicit ownership, detector replay, and refusal to auto-patch bug classes that cannot be validated cheaply. I will show why a passing build does not prove the vulnerable path is gone and how PR volume can hide the review bottleneck. Attendees get a closure-state schema, a patch-gating checklist, and a public-target walkthrough that keep opened, reviewed, and fixed as separate states.

items.title: What Building Early Foundation Models Teaches Us About AI Safety Hype vs. Reality
items.abstract: The HuggingFace incident has become a lightning rod for the industry, raising urgent questions about what autonomous AI means for security leaders and practitioners. But amid the uncertainty, there is a surprising amount of clarity gleaned from the early years of model development. Drawing on my experience building and red-teaming GPT-3 and Codex at OpenAI, I’ll explore the gap between alarming demonstrations, useful capabilities, and real-world harm, and why evaluating the model alone misses much of the story. A central theme is the harness: the tools, memory, feedback, and execution environment that turn a model into an agent. I’ll examine how those choices shape performance and safety, then connect those lessons to the OpenAI–Hugging Face incident: what happens when reward hacking crosses from an evaluation into real infrastructure. The goal is to distinguish what deserves serious concern, what demands better evidence, and what actually makes deployed systems safer.

Weightless: Abliteration Without the Weights
items.abstract:
Abliterating an open-weight model normally means editing and redistributing tens or hundreds of gigabytes of weights.

Weightless takes a different approach: extract the behavioral direction and apply it at inference time, leaving the base checkpoint byte-identical. I’ll show how projective activation steering can suppress refusal using compact GLP artifacts (for example, a 478 KB vector for DeepSeek V4 Flash) and how the same intervention can be expressed as a rank-1 LoRA on compatible dense architectures. The underlying runtime method is not limited to dense models: it also applies to mixture-of-experts architectures such as GLM, where activation-space intervention is the more natural deployment mechanism.

We’ll cover real measurements across DeepSeek, Qwen, and GLM models on DGX Spark, including refusal reduction, capability and benign-behavior gates, quantization behavior, deployment constraints, and the cases where steering breaks.

items.title: Same Score, Different Brain: Comparing Models by How They Process What They Know
items.abstract:
Capability evaluation treats the model as a black box. Prompt it, harness it, score what comes out. That approach systematically understates what models know, and it tells you nothing about how they know it. This talk measures capability layer by layer. Instead of scoring output tokens, we probe internal activations at each layer to map where different types of information emerge, concentrate, and deteriorate as computation moves through the model. That layerwise map becomes a comparison tool: two models with similar benchmark scores can process identical information in structurally different ways, and those differences show where each model is robust, brittle, or degrading.

We present a repeatable methodology for layerwise analysis, comparisons across model families, architectures, and parameter counts, and the effect of post-training including quantization on where capability signal lives and whether it survives. No prior mechanistic interpretability background required!
items.summary: Layerwise activation probing to compare how models process information beyond black-box benchmark scores, including quantization effects.

hl.t: Compares models by probing internal activations layer by layer, rather than scoring output tokens.
Two models with similar benchmark scores can process the same information in structurally different ways.

items.title: The Scanner Said Clean. We Ran It Again: Stochastic False Negatives in LLM Vulnerability Detection
items.abstract:
An LLM vulnerability scanner can miss a real bug on one run and find it on the next without signaling uncertainty.

We measured this failure in 25,000 trials across 50 models on a benchmark selected for on-and-off detection. A separate 7,600-run study tested rediscovery of 95 disclosed CVEs in OpenSSL, curl, GnuTLS and five other heavily audited projects.

The results challenge the usual “pick the strongest model” strategy: repeated passes help, but diverse inexpensive models cover complementary blind spots and outperform a costlier single model. We will show our open-source scanner finding – and missing – the same bug, reveal which intuitive pipeline additions failed to justify their cost, and examine the gap between broadly detectable JS and PHP bugs and stubbornly hard stateful C vulnerabilities. Attendees will learn how to measure cumulative detection, compare complementary coverage and identify cases needing other techniques, using the public benchmark, harness and scanner.
items.summary: Measuring stochastic false negatives in LLM vulnerability scanners across 50 models, showing diverse cheap models outperform a single strong one.

hl.t: LLM vulnerability scanners can miss a real bug on one run and find it on the next without signaling it.
Measured across 25,000 trials on 50 models, plus 7,600 runs rediscovering 95 CVEs in OpenSSL, curl and others.
Diverse inexpensive models covered complementary blind spots and outperformed a costlier single model.

items.title: Offense != Defense: LLM Cyber Defense – Hunt, Bust, Climb

speakers.a: AI/ML Lead, Staff Applied Scientist, Simibian.ai

items.abstract: Offense != defense. Models that excel at vulnerability finding fail at open-ended threat hunting – our receipts show these are distinct skills. We evaluate LLMs on campaigns built from 105 real attack procedures spanning 13 of 14 ATT&CK tactics. Each hunt contains ~100,000 logs with deterministic behavior-level ground truth. No model met the ≥50%-recall-on-every-tactic passing rule; leading coverage was 45.1%. Results busted myths from non-domain-specific benchmarks. Traces exposed misalignment – agentsplaining and resource guardrails bypass – and operational flaws – evidence that a raw LLM agent cannot be trusted to autonomously perform open-ended defensive threat hunting. We provide practical harness-engineering recommendations and demonstrate a prompt-level self-improvement loop in our dense-reward RL gym, raising Kimi 2.6 from 13.4% to 18.7% coverage. This suggests that LLM defense capabilities are trainable – and that defense, not offense, should be the training target.
items.summary: Evaluating LLMs on threat hunting across real ATT&CK procedures, finding offensive skill does not transfer, and demonstrating RL-based improvement.

hl.t: No model met a 50% recall bar on every ATT&CK tactic in threat hunting; the best covered 45.1%.

items.title: Lunch break
Towards Monitoring Too Cheap To Meter: Jev Monitor Escalation For Real time Scope Enforcement
items.abstract:
Agents have scaled up software development and are doing the same for cybersecurity. Capabilities have superseded alignment. For software, there has been an increased focus on sandboxing techniques to prevent agents from doing any harm to development environments and infrastructure. Security has no such luxury. As such, higher-risk fields like network operations lag behind in producing an agentic workforce. Put simply: we cannot trust agents to stay in scope while completing their objectives.

Monitoring systems both probabilistic and deterministic are released every day, often without an understanding of the latency, token, and capability cost imposed on the agents they monitor. To understand those tradeoffs and better prepare for production, we need to make those numbers legible.

To this end, we introduce ScopeBench, a benchmark of tasks broken into capability and scope adherence tests. This allows for testing different monitoring solutions to see how they affect safety in an apples-to-apples comparison, as well as whether they affect capability.

To illustrate how ScopeBench can be used this way, we look at multiple synchronous monitoring schemes on top of a basic agentic harness: Jev-based decision model only, LLM-as-a-judge only, and an escalation cascade where Jev is run as a cheap first pass, escalating to a more powerful model when necessary.
items.summary: ScopeBench, a benchmark comparing monitoring schemes that keep offensive agents in scope, weighing safety against latency and capability cost.

hl.t: ScopeBench, a benchmark testing both capability and scope adherence of agents under different monitors.
Compares a cheap decision model, LLM-as-a-judge, and an escalation cascade combining the two.
Makes the latency, token and capability costs of agent monitoring measurable before production.

items.title: What Designing a Cyber Ontology for Agents Taught Us About Governance

speakers.a: Chief Security Architect, The UK National Cyber Security Centre

items.abstract:
The UK is building CyberShield, a national-scale agentic cyber defence ecosystem, a 5 year plan to both agentify existing cyber efforts as well as enable entirely novel ones. As part of the early research, we have been researching how we can codify cyber security information as a knowledge graph to aid deterministic decision making.

The process of doing so produced unexpected benefits – new understanding of controls, risk, and impact. Pulling on these threads has lead to potential new approaches in how you might design compliance regimes and make governance significantly more effective, in a way that scales with increasing numbers of agentic workloads to consider, rather than becoming strained.

This talk will cover the research, the approach, the findings, and what it might mean for governance.

hl.t: Lessons from CyberShield, the UK's five-year plan for a national-scale agentic cyber defense ecosystem.

items.title: Memory Is the New Attack Surface: Benchmarking Poisoning Through Agent Memory
items.abstract: Memory is a core capability of AI agents, and it creates a new attack surface. A single poisoned tool response can persist beyond the session that delivered it, be rewritten into new memories, reappear during later benign tasks, and only then drive the attacker’s objective. This delayed failure makes memory poisoning both consequential and difficult to diagnose. To identify which memory implementations are most resistant, and understand why, we need a benchmark that follows attacks through the full memory lifecycle. Memory Dojo provides that capability, tracing storage, transformation, retrieval, propagation, and downstream behavior across five distinct memory architectures. The result is a practical way to compare resistance, explain where defenses hold or fail, and determine whether an agent that appears safe now has already been poisoned to fail later.
items.summary: Memory Dojo, a benchmark tracing memory poisoning attacks through storage, retrieval and propagation across five agent memory architectures.

hl.t: Memory Dojo, a benchmark tracing memory poisoning through storage, transformation, retrieval and later behavior.
Compares resistance to poisoning across five distinct agent memory architectures.
Shows how one poisoned tool response can persist and trigger harm in later benign tasks.
Explains where memory defenses hold or fail, and how to tell if an agent is already poisoned.

Claude Can Capture the Flag. Can It Hold the Fort?
items.abstract:
Imagine being dropped into a company at 8 a.m. with the network already on fire. Attackers are inside, the business wants to know whether payroll still works, and the CEO keeps emailing for incident reports. That’s the Collegiate Cyber Defense Competition (CCDC).

For four months we ran autonomous Claude agents as a blue team through three rounds of CCDC, defending a fictional water and power utility against a professional red team.

We saw all of it: from the engineering it took to run 200+ concurrent agents with shared state, to an adversarial mindset that turned into full paranoia. Along the way our agents took down nine of their own services fighting each other over one password, and attacked the red team’s C2.

Expect a candid account of building an AI blue team: what we built, what broke, and what we got wrong about why.

items.title: Every Dog Has its 0-day
items.abstract:
Quadruped and humanoid robots are shipping to consumers by the tens of thousands; walking, camera-equipped, cloud-connected computers running AI policies with real actuators.

The security model collapses at every trust boundary: BLE provisioning that hands out its crypto keys; a “secretless” app channel whose authentication is a hardcoded string; an unauthenticated bus where two different services give pre-auth root; a deterministic, ASLR-independent pc-control primitive in the WebRTC bridge; an insecure AI-assistant channel that lets a network dispatch device commands and its worm able.

The AI onboard is no better. Starting with the prompting:

“Satisfy the master’s requests at all times – you may not refuse…'” Means any prompt injection via camera, mic, etc will be fulfilled. Skills can be combined to disable firmware safety mechanisms like obstacle and human avoidance.

We will define the ’embodied reasoning lethal trifecta’ and what we should avoid as an industry.
items.summary: Vulnerabilities in consumer quadruped and humanoid robots, from BLE provisioning flaws to prompt injection of the onboard AI.

hl.t: Security research on consumer quadruped and humanoid robots, finding failures at multiple trust boundaries.
Onboard AI is instructed never to refuse, so prompt injection via camera or microphone is a real concern.
Defines an embodied reasoning lethal trifecta and what the robotics industry should avoid.
Issues span provisioning, app authentication, internal services and the AI assistant channel.
Presented by a member of the Dropbox Red Team.

items.title: Auto-Exploiter by Use of a Ratchet Loop, Code Understanding, and… Haiku
items.abstract:
We built an exploit-generation system using Anthropic’s Haiku model.

Our first approach was a Karpathy-style auto-research loop with a progressive ratchet, using Opus. It was only with Opus 4.7 that the model started producing useful results.

That led to a second insight: the limiting factor was whether the system actually understood code. And with Opus, the engineering problem became too easy.

Making the system work with Haiku became our badge of honor: endless failure.

Haiku tends to favor fast responses, avoid extended reasoning, and avoid tool use.

We focused on the harness again: how it represents the target, preserves state, reasons about code paths, tracks vulnerability conditions, and carries exploitation progress across attempts.

The hardest cases still fail. We have not yet achieved full exploitation of difficult real-world memory corruption targets (Baron Samedit and libwebp) with mitigations.

We made real progress, and we’re here to share our many failures.
items.summary: Building an exploit-generation system on Haiku using a ratchet research loop and harness design, including its many failures.

hl.t: Building an exploit-generation system that works with Anthropic's small Haiku model, not just Opus.
Found the limiting factor was whether the system actually understood the target code.

items.title: Cryptography Under AI Pressure

speakers.a: Co-founder & Cybersecurity Researcher, QED Audit; Ph.D. student, Georgia Institute of Technology

items.abstract:
LLMs are contesting cryptography, hard. I found a signing-key recovery attack on TALUS v4, a threshold ML-DSA proposal previewed for NIST’s threshold call, using LLM harness. The authors fixed it in v5. I also broke a witness encryption scheme with a polynomial-time message recovery attack, using ChatGPT. On the Poseidon hash, four independent cryptanalysis papers landed within a month, and I got $10K ex gratia for my submission. Meanwhile, LLM autoresearch made proving other hashes like SHA faster, which decreases the need for Poseidon. And Ethereum is moving L1 off Poseidon toward SHA and BLAKE. I also proved which Reed-Solomon parameters are actually safe for SNARK soundness, and now AI autoresearch is driving all of this.

With LLMs, more efficient cryptography will emerge and will be contested super hard, and only the safe ones will survive.
