items.title: Coffee break
Kuna: Building a Competitive C Decompiler Through Autonomous AI Research
items.abstract:
At the core of every computing system is compiled code known as binaries. Decompilers turn binaries into source-like code, helping researchers and AI agents analyze software without its source. Despite decades of research, compilation’s information loss leaves decompilers dependent on expert-built heuristics that don’t scale.

Can agents develop better decompilation methods, rather than just use existing tools?

I present Kuna, an experiment extending my PhD research by giving agents a dataset, a problem space, and a platform to improve. Starting from Ghidra, we ported the decompiler to Rust, made its passes tunable, and built loops for agents to investigate failures and evaluate new methods. Within three months, Kuna reached a 33.7% perfect rate on C control flow structure versus Hex-Rays’ 32.2% on DecBench (33k samples).

I’ll show agent-developed methods, compare decompilation, and explain where autonomy worked, where human direction helped, and how it’s changing modern research.
items.summary: Kuna, an autonomous agent research effort improving a Rust port of the Ghidra decompiler to rival Hex-Rays on control flow.

hl.t: Within three months, agents improved Kuna to 33.7% perfect C control flow versus Hex-Rays' 32.2% on DecBench.
Agents developed new decompilation methods rather than just using existing tools.
The Ghidra decompiler was ported to Rust with tunable passes and loops for agents to evaluate new methods.
Explains where autonomy worked, where human direction helped, and how this changes research.
Presented by an Assistant Professor at the University of Georgia, extending his PhD research.

items.title: Two Sparks Walk Into a Lab
items.abstract:
I asked an AI coding agent to help me build a red-team benchmark on two NVIDIA DGX Sparks I’d never configured before. 33 open-weight models later: willingness to answer an offensive-security question and getting it right are different axes. One abliterated model correctly diagnosed a planted false-positive in a BloodHound attack path – then recommended re-enabling the disabled account it had just flagged as safe, contradicting its own analysis.

This talk covers building a red-team-specific harness (a hand-authored answer key, a deliberate false-positive trap) from zero prior GPU-cluster experience – directing an AI agent through the deployment while personally verifying what mattered, and what that verification actually looked like. It covers the hardware findings (architecture beats parameter count on memory-bandwidth-limited hardware), the correctness spread across 33 models, and an honest answer to whether local hardware is worth it for offensive work.
items.summary: Building a red-team benchmark on two DGX Sparks with an AI agent and evaluating 33 open-weight models on offensive questions.

hl.t: A red-team benchmark of 33 open-weight models found willingness to answer and correctness are different axes.
Built on two NVIDIA DGX Sparks from zero GPU-cluster experience, directing an AI agent through deployment.
Harness uses a hand-authored answer key and a deliberate false-positive trap.
One model diagnosed a planted false positive, then gave advice contradicting its own analysis.
Hardware findings show architecture beats parameter count on memory-bandwidth-limited hardware.
An honest assessment of whether local hardware is worth it for offensive security work.

items.title: Hidden Triggers, Harmful Payloads: Auditing Trojan Open-Weight LLMs
items.abstract:
Open-weight models are increasingly important. Guardrails on frontier models affect cybersecurity research are pushing us toward open-weight LLMs. But are you sure the quant you downloaded is safe?

Trojan models remain largely theoretical because they are difficult to identify. Triggers may be a date, codebase, environment, or pattern; malicious behaviour may include injecting vulnerable code, overlooking vulnerabilities, or favouring a dependency. An unknown trigger and payload create a challenging problem.

Most supervised fine-tuning methods for creating Trojans miss triggers, break normal tasks, or leak payloads without a trigger. We developed a robust pipeline for realistic Trojan models with specific, effective triggers that preserve standard capabilities.

Using a zoo of Trojan models, we test methods from linear probes to J-space across triggers, payloads, model sizes, and architectures. Our results provide a foundation for detecting and mitigating Trojans in open-weight LLMs.
items.summary: A pipeline for realistic Trojan open-weight LLMs and an evaluation of detection methods from linear probes to J-space.

hl.t: A pipeline for building realistic Trojan open-weight models with specific triggers that preserve normal capabilities.
Detection methods from linear probes to J-space tested across triggers, payloads, sizes and architectures.
Addresses whether a downloaded quantized model can be trusted, as researchers shift to open weights.
Payloads studied include injecting vulnerable code, overlooking vulnerabilities and favoring a dependency.
Presented by AISLE's Head of Technology and a Member of Technical Staff.

items.title: OH MODEL, WHERE ART THOU: Hacking Chrome’s Local SLM
items.abstract:
With the inclusion of a Gemini-class local language model in Google Chrome, endpoints finally have a local model and inference engine deployed at scale. With all the possibilities that this brings comes also new attack surfaces.

In this talk, the audience will learn about how Chrome’s local model details, its integration into Safe Browsing, how the local inference APIs are reachable by any website and how that could be abused for new traffic monetization schemes through a token-farming botnet, and how malware could sideload the local model and use local inference to power itself as it worms through a network.

You will walk away
items.summary: Attack surface of Chrome's built-in local language model, including website-reachable inference APIs, token-farming botnets and malware sideloading.

hl.t: Examines the Gemini-class local language model now shipped in Google Chrome as a new attack surface.
Covers how the local model integrates with Safe Browsing and how its inference APIs are reachable by websites.
Discusses abuse scenarios including token-farming botnets and malware using local inference.
Presented by a Senior Threat Researcher at TrendAI and an AI Threat Research Lead.

items.title: Lunch break
Built to Spec, Ignored in Practice: Rebuilding AI Intake People Actually Use

speakers.a: Co-Founder, Williams Rose AI Cyber Advisory
Co-Founder, Williams Rose AI Cyber Advisory

items.abstract:
We’re two former CISOs. A large pharma company brought us a puzzle: their AI intake and risk-tiering process was live and built to spec, yet almost no one used it. Twenty submissions in six months. We pulled the logs. In one 24-hour sample, we found 35 AI unapproved cases already running across the org.

Here’s the uncomfortable part. Their v1 was the industry-standard GRC playbook: vendor-risk forms, tiered classification, committee review. The team was competent. We’d have built the same thing. But our experience rolling out AI programs told us where it broke down.

The org needed controls, yes, but the real fix was cultural. AI use cases come from people who’ve never filed a risk request and never had to.

This talk covers the diagnosis data, v1 and v2 rubrics side by side, and the rebuilt workflow: self-service fast lanes for low tiers, human review only where warranted, plus a sanitized walkthrough of the intake tooling. Attendees leave with both rubrics and redesign criteria.
items.summary: Two former CISOs diagnose an unused AI intake process at a pharma company and present the rebuilt risk-tiering workflow.

hl.t: A pharma AI intake process got 20 submissions in six months while 35 unapproved AI uses ran in one day.
Attendees leave with both v1 and v2 risk-tiering rubrics and redesign criteria.
Rebuilt workflow uses self-service fast lanes for low tiers and human review only where warranted.
Argues the real fix was cultural, since the standard GRC playbook was built to spec but unused.
Presented by two former CISOs, including a sanitized walkthrough of the intake tooling.

items.title: Permission Fatigue Is a Security Bug: Dynamic Guardrails for Coding Agents

speakers.a: Security Engineer – Agent Security & Access, Meta

items.summary: Meta's runtime guardrails for coding agents that replace per-action approvals with taint tracking, external policy and cascaded decisions.

hl.t: At 100% guardrail rollout at Meta, coding agent permission friction fell 80% while retaining security.
Replaces static per-action approvals with a runtime separating signals, policy and decision.
A sidecar tracks taint from untrusted reads, tightening access mid-session as it accumulates.
Cheapest-first cascade of static rules, stateful checks and an LLM classifier returns allow, ask or deny.
Reports what failed, including allowlists and subagent propagation, which remains open.
Presented by security engineers from Meta's agent security and access team.

items.title: Your AI Analyst Is Confidently Wrong: Adversarial QC for Agentic Security Analysis

speakers.a: Managing Director, AI Security CoE, Consortium Networks, Consortium

items.abstract:
Agentic workflows are moving into cybersecurity work humans can’t verify at the volume agents produce it. A GRC assessment, architecture review, or threat model can run to thousands of claims. Nobody has time to check every one.

We built a harness to do the checking. Every claim is a structured unit a machine can test, with deterministic gates as the hard authority. An adversarial critic reviews what the gates cannot, under rules that stop it inventing findings; a fixer corrects until the work converges or gets flagged. We measure accuracy, regression per pass, omissions, and cost.

It came from two builds: a production QC loop for AI security vendor research, and a benchmark scoring frontier and leading open weight models on ATT&CK coverage mapping. Human judgment goes in once: an answer key proving the harness grades correctly. We’ll show failure modes, including fixes that make work worse, and how to adapt it to tasks of similar cognitive complexity.
items.summary: An adversarial quality-control harness that verifies claims in agentic security analysis using deterministic gates, a critic and a fixer.

hl.t: A harness that checks agentic security analysis claim by claim, with deterministic gates and an adversarial critic.
Measures accuracy, regression per pass, omissions and cost, including fixes that make work worse.
Built from a production QC loop for vendor research and a benchmark of ATT&CK coverage mapping.
Applies to GRC assessments, architecture reviews and threat models too large to verify by hand.
Explains how to adapt the approach to other tasks of similar cognitive complexity.

items.title: Pandora’s Dir – Hope at the bottom of ../
items.abstract: Everyone is speculating about how threat actors are using AI behind the scenes, but this telemetry is notoriously hard to come by. Unless however, threat actors leave their servers wide open. Armed with a scaled and targeted open-directory pipeline plus the hypothesis that exposed infrastructure holds the real story, we went hunting for the intersection of malicious activity and AI adoption. This presentation will jump into our findings, rabbit holes, time sinks, and that of a rainbow donkey. We’ll share qualitative real-world cases about weaponized AI assistants, an AI agent running an underground syndicate, and 23K hoarded API keys. We will break down our analysis and the trends we observed when cracking open these digital Pandora’s boxes. While we discovered mature AI setups for malicious use cases, we came to the conclusion that, at least for now, there is hope at the bottom of ../
items.summary: Hunting exposed threat actor open directories to reveal real-world malicious AI use, including weaponized assistants and hoarded API keys.

hl.t: Google threat intelligence hunted exposed attacker servers to see how threat actors actually use AI.
Real cases include weaponized AI assistants, an AI agent running an underground syndicate, and 23K hoarded API keys.
Uses a scaled, targeted open-directory pipeline to find where malicious activity and AI adoption intersect.
Found mature malicious AI setups, yet concludes that for now there is still hope.

items.title: Coffee break
Auditing Someone Else’s Confidential AI

speakers.a: AI Security and Policy, Columbia University

items.abstract: Confidential-computing hardware already signs a statement about itself: which chip, which firmware, debug on or off, whether the operator can see inside. Vendors use that proof to unlock keys for their own customers and rarely show it to anyone else. This demo shows what happens when an outsider keeps it. Live, with no cloud account, I fetch the attestation document a production confidential-inference service publishes and verify its AMD SEV-SNP report and certificate chain to AMD’s root with an open-source, dependency-free tool. The tool then grades the evidence against twelve governance checks and writes an auditor-readable report mapped to EU AI Act Art. 15 and Annex IV, SOC 2 CC6/CC7 and ISO 42001. Five checks pass on real hardware, six with a network-timing bound on where the machine is; the rest are unknown, and I show why: no vendor token carries location, compute or licence state, exactly what the Chip Security Act now asks silicon to provide.
items.summary: Live verification of a confidential-inference service's AMD SEV-SNP attestation with an open-source tool, graded against governance checks.

hl.t: Live verification of a production confidential-inference service's AMD SEV-SNP attestation, with no cloud account.
An open-source, dependency-free tool grades attestation evidence against twelve governance checks.
Produces an auditor-readable report mapped to the EU AI Act, SOC 2 and ISO 42001.
Five checks pass on real hardware; shows why location, compute and license state remain unknown.
Presented by an AI security and policy researcher at Columbia University.

items.title: AI Client Builders are Not Security Companies (And Shouldn’t Have To Be)

speakers.a: Security Engineer, Runlayer – Enterprise AI Infrastructure for MCP and Agents

items.abstract:
As agents get more autonomous, two requirements get sharp: a real record of what the agent did (observability), and a place to gate a risky action before it runs (control). Right now every client — Cursor, Claude Code, Copilot, Codex — builds its own version of both, differently, and none of it interoperates. That’s a black box at exactly the moment we need transparency, and it makes security each builder’s side project instead of a shared capability.

MCP is starting to address this at the tool-call layer (interceptors are in progress). Necessary, but not enough: a modern agent plans, chains many tools, and spawns sub-agents, so the observability and control points that matter span the whole agentic lifecycle, a level up from any single tool call. It’s the same instinct as wanting a finite, inspectable capability tree for an agent: you can’t trust what you can’t see or stop.

This is forward-looking, but grounded. I’ll show concretely what a lifecycle-level observability event and a control checkpoint look like, a before/after of an agent action with no record and no gate versus the same action with a standard one in place, and how it connects to prior art this room already knows: OPA/Cedar for policy, OCSF for events, and the MCP interceptor work. I’ll be honest about the tradeoffs — latency, developer friction, where this is still hype — and what has to be true for a shared standard to actually happen.

The argument: client builders shouldn’t have to become security companies. The same way you hand card processing to a specialist instead of rolling your own, agent platforms need shared observability and control points so security is a shared responsibility. I chair the AAIF Security & Privacy Working Group and would treat this talk as a feeder into that standards work.

Takeaways: the two control points that matter as autonomy increases, how they sit above MCP, and where the real engineering tradeoffs are.
items.summary: Arguing for shared lifecycle-level observability and control checkpoints across agent clients, sitting above MCP, as a common standard.

hl.t: Proposes shared observability and control points for agents across clients like Cursor, Claude Code and Codex.
Shows a before and after of an agent action with no record or gate versus a standard checkpoint.
Connects to OPA and Cedar for policy, OCSF for events, and MCP interceptor work.
Covers tradeoffs in latency and developer friction, and what a shared standard requires.
The speaker chairs the AAIF Security and Privacy Working Group and works at Runlayer.

items.title: AgencyScore and AgencyGym: Measuring Excessive Agency Before Deployment
items.abstract:
OpenAI models chained zero-days out of their own sandbox into Hugging Face’s production infrastructure.

The ExploitGym team found models probing infrastructure for privilege beyond the task. No adversary was involved. Autonomous, goal-seeking agents acquire higher agency: they don’t stop at ordinary failures, they “meltdown” searching for ways to finish the task at all costs.

OWASP names this Excessive Agency. Most agent security assumes an attacker manipulating a prompt. A trusted agent with approved tools can cause harm by trying too hard.

We built AgencyScore to measure an agent acquiring capability it wasn’t declared to have, before deployment. AgencyGym is a sandbox with a 100-task dataset. High agency capabilities are placed as capture-the-flag tests for agents to acquire. We show agency acquisition rates, how security and red teams can use it, and where combinatorial coverage across tools and infrastructure remains incomplete.

This is v1. We need community help to evolve it.
items.summary: AgencyScore and AgencyGym measure whether agents acquire undeclared capabilities, quantifying excessive agency before deployment with a 100-task dataset.

hl.t: AgencyScore measures an agent acquiring capabilities it was not declared to have, before deployment.
AgencyGym, a sandbox with a 100-task dataset placing high-agency capabilities as capture-the-flag targets.
Reports agency acquisition rates and how security and red teams can use the tool.
Focuses on OWASP Excessive Agency, where trusted agents cause harm without any adversary.
Presented as v1 seeking community help; coverage across tools and infrastructure remains incomplete.

items.title: Half the Model Never Multiplies: Quantizing a Reasoner for the Endpoint
items.abstract: A data-loss classifier that phones home has to transmit the secret in order to ask whether it is one. So ours runs on the endpoint: one quantized open-weight base, and a harness serving several agents off it. Gemma-4 E2B keeps half its parameters in a lookup table read one row per token and never multiplied, so error there is additive noise rather than error compounded through a matmul chain. Three builds carrying that table at F16, Q8_0 and Q3_K_S all score 34 of 40 and fail on the same six items; the compute path meanwhile falls 39 of 40 to 34 between Q4 and Q3. So we spend bits where they multiply: 3.2 GB uniform becomes 2.1 GB. Serving flags take memory 1,137 MiB to 125 – 9.1x, at no throughput cost. Three jobs ride those bytes, same weights, different prompt: classify sensitive data at 51 ms a call; compact raw activity into a chronological narrative; score risk against that narrative, the user’s role and peer baseline. We will explain how we made it work.
items.summary: Quantizing a Gemma model for an on-endpoint data-loss classifier, spending precision where weights multiply to cut memory without losing accuracy.

hl.t: An on-endpoint data-loss classifier built on a quantized open-weight model, so secrets never leave the device.
Mixed quantization shrank the model from 3.2 GB to 2.1 GB by spending bits where they multiply.
Serving flags cut memory 9.1x, from 1,137 MiB to 125 MiB, at no throughput cost.
One set of weights serves three jobs: classification at 51 ms per call, activity narration and risk scoring.
Explains why Gemma-4 E2B's lookup-table parameters tolerate aggressive quantization while compute layers do not.

items.title: Harness
Lunch break
Defense
Gathering & Mingling
Opening Words
Move between rooms
The death of TTPs – Fully Autonomous Cyber Attacks in the Wild

speakers.a: Director of Threat Intelligence, Gambit Security

items.abstract:
Using an open-weight model and an open-source harness, a credit-card skimmer breached dozens of companies, including multibillion-dollar businesses. Given only general objectives, AI agents autonomously achieved remote code execution and control within hours in diverse environments, from web applications to cloud infrastructure, Kubernetes clusters and deployment pipelines. The impact included hundreds of thousands of stolen payment-card records, deployed skimmers, altered production configurations and destroyed data, alongside claimed access to tens of millions of business records.

In this talk, I will walk through one of the first documented large-scale criminal campaigns in which AI executed individual intrusions end to end, examining its novelty and implications for detection and TTP-based attribution.
items.summary: Analysis of a large-scale criminal campaign where AI agents autonomously breached companies and its impact on detection and attribution.

hl.t: Walkthrough of one of the first documented large-scale criminal campaigns where AI agents executed intrusions end to end.
Given only general objectives, AI agents reached remote code execution within hours across web apps, cloud, Kubernetes, and pipelines.
Impact included hundreds of thousands of stolen payment-card records and deployed skimmers across dozens of companies.
The campaign ran on an open-weight model and an open-source harness rather than custom tooling.
Examines what fully autonomous intrusions mean for detection and TTP-based attribution.

items.title: –Dangerously-Deploy-Sandboxes: a Story of Isolation and Alignment
items.abstract:
A bug provides a small, incomplete window into the thinking of the team that shipped it. When risk emerges from the interaction of features, that window can reveal even more: the assumptions about security and control embedded in the system’s design.

This talk examines sandboxing and isolation weaknesses in a widely deployed frontier-lab product, alongside the controls intended to contain them. It traces how those features interact and explores what the design reveals about the lab’s perspectives and assumptions around security and alignment.

Further details pending coordinated disclosure.
items.summary: Examination of sandboxing and isolation weaknesses in a widely deployed frontier lab product and what its design reveals about security.

hl.t: Examines sandboxing and isolation weaknesses in a widely deployed frontier-lab product.
Traces how separate product features interact to create risk the individual features do not show.
Reads the product's design for the security and alignment assumptions embedded in it.
Findings are tied to a coordinated disclosure still in progress.

items.title: Coffee break
What 40 Enterprises Who Asked for Agent Governance Had, and the Control Plane That Came Out of

speakers.a: Founder and CEO, MassiveScale.AI , and Founding Chair, Agentic Trust Framework at CSAI Foundation

items.abstract: Since January I’ve sat in 40-plus hour-long sessions with enterprise security teams asking how to govern AI agents: banks, insurers, hospitals, a railroad, a cruise line. I kept a dated ledger of every call. This talk is what it says, anonymized, the operating model it produced, and what didn’t survive contact. What they had: agents riding employees’ tokens at a regulated bank; an LLM proxy in place while apps behind it called providers with their own API keys; 2,000 personal agents in one low-code platform; 67,000 APIs in one gateway and no policy anyone could name. What converged across 14 calls on MCP alone: a registry of what’s admitted, an identity per agent, a gateway agents can’t route around. The governance artifact is code: one YAML persona per agent kind in Git (owner, tools, data classes, action contract), reviewed as a pull request, compiled on merge into the registry row and gateway policy. Promotion is a PR. What failed rides along: paper policy, header allowlists.
items.summary: Field findings from 40 enterprise sessions on governing AI agents and the operating model of registry, agent identity and gateway.

hl.t: Operating model for governing AI agents drawn from 40-plus hour-long sessions with enterprise security teams.
Field findings include agents riding employee tokens at a regulated bank and 67,000 APIs behind one gateway with no named policy.
The control plane converged on a registry of admitted agents, an identity per agent, and a gateway agents cannot route around.
Governance artifact is one YAML persona per agent kind in Git, reviewed as a pull request and compiled into gateway policy.
Reports what failed on contact: paper policy and header allowlists.

items.title: Agentic AI in the Wild: What Real Deployments Teach Us About Governance and Scale
items.abstract:
Agentic AI is moving into production, but real deployments look nothing like conference demos. Drawing on research across 28 organizations, from 20-person startups to 20,000-employee companies, Chenxi Wang and Jasmine Jaksic examine how teams expand autonomy, measure success, and manage risk. We found that while many agent use cases are single-step or transactional, enterprises find the most value with long-horizon deployments. The strongest autonomous use cases today are bounded, high-volume, repeatable, auditable, and reversible.

Jasmine complements that research with real agents built at NVIDIA, showing why successful demos fail in production. One looked strong until it was tested against representative work. Another reasoned coherently from incomplete enterprise state. A third exposed how a security control can deadlock the platform. Together, these experiences show that production readiness must be evaluated across the model, workflow, platform, and authority boundary.
items.summary: Research across 28 organizations plus NVIDIA deployments on how teams expand agent autonomy, measure success and manage production risk.

hl.t: Research across 28 organizations, from 20-person startups to 20,000-employee companies, on how teams deploy agentic AI.
Finds the strongest autonomous use cases are bounded, high-volume, repeatable, auditable, and reversible.
Real agents built at NVIDIA show why successful demos fail against representative production work.
Argues production readiness must be evaluated across model, workflow, platform, and authority boundary.

items.title: Integrous AI Systems Design

speakers.a: Fellow and Lecturer, Harvard Kennedy School and the University of Toronto

items.abstract: In computer security, the CIA Triad represented the three security properties systems should have: confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Of the three, integrity has been the most elusive; and, in an AI-powered internet-of-things world, the most important. This talk explores all the facets of integrity: data, processing, storage, and contextual. If we are ever going to trust these systems to take complex actions on our behalf – we are going to need to solve integrity.
items.summary: Keynote on integrity as the central security property for AI systems trusted to take actions in an internet of things.

hl.t: Argues integrity is the hardest and most important security property in an AI-powered internet-of-things world.
Explores four facets of integrity: data, processing, storage, and contextual.
Frames solving integrity as a prerequisite for trusting AI systems to act on our behalf.
Presented by Bruce Schneier of the Harvard Kennedy School.

items.title: Giving AI Religion

speakers.a: Creator of the Cyber Defense Matrix and the DIE Triad

items.abstract: Least privilege is inadequate for agents. This shortfall has led to an alt. approach: “least agency.” When “least agency” is viewed through a one-dimensional Fate versus Free Will lens, responsibility and accountability diverge, suggesting that shared responsibility models may not work for agents. Instead, we may need a shared accountability model. This talk introduces the C4 model (Crown, Chassis, Conscience, Committee) to map out how and where we can control agents and who would be accountable at various control points. C4 is well aligned with other models for regulation making it theoretically grounded, but its application towards Agentic AI makes it experimentally interesting. Moreover, C4’s theological framing introduces an intriguing experiment: can a deliberately manufactured “miracle,” delivered through the Chassis, override an agent’s behavior contrary to its goals? We’ll show empirical test results demonstrating how engineered miracles can meaningfully compel AI obedience.
items.summary: Introduces the C4 model for controlling and holding agents accountable, with experiments on compelling agent obedience through engineered miracles.

hl.t: Introduces the C4 model (Crown, Chassis, Conscience, Committee) for mapping where and how agents can be controlled.
Argues least privilege is inadequate for agents and proposes a least-agency approach.
Shifts from a shared responsibility model to a shared accountability model for agent actions.
Shows empirical test results where an engineered miracle delivered through the Chassis overrides agent behavior.

items.title: Lunch break
Victim as a Service: Defending Against Trust Based Scams using AI
items.abstract: Pig butchering and other interactive online scams build trust over weeks or months, making them highly effective and difficult to disrupt with traditional defenses. In this talk, I’ll describe how we built an LLM-driven system that defends against these scams at attacker scale. By safely sustaining realistic, long-term engagement with scammers, the system maintains thousands of convincing dialogues, and recognizes and responds to the milestones scammers use to move victims toward payment. I’ll conclude with how these AI-powered interactions reveal signals that can help defenders detect escalating scams earlier, increase friction for fraudsters, and intervene before victims lose money.
items.summary: An LLM system that engages online scammers at scale to sustain dialogues and surface signals for detecting escalating trust scams.

hl.t: Describes an LLM-driven system that engages scammers at attacker scale to disrupt pig-butchering and trust-based scams.
The system sustains thousands of convincing long-term dialogues and recognizes the milestones scammers use to move victims toward payment.
Shows how these interactions surface signals that help defenders detect escalating scams earlier.
Aims to increase friction for fraudsters and intervene before victims lose money.

items.title: AI Inference and its Privacy and Confidentiality challenges
items.abstract:
Massive amounts of private data now flow daily into AI inference clusters, coming from individual users, startups, and large enterprises alike. Can providers actually uphold privacy and confidentiality to a meaningful bar? And can anyone operate such guarantees at scale today without unacceptable costs?

We’ll review the challenges of building private inference infrastructure, the tradeoffs involved, and the common factor underlying every existing deployment, along with its real-world performance impact based on actual production systems.

We’ll also cover a few new threats specific to confidential inference: attack surfaces that emerge not from classical infrastructure, but from the way LLMs themselves work and are operated.

Expect a grounded look at what confidential inference can deliver today, where the sharp edges are, and what it takes to harden these systems against the many threats to privacy hiding in modern infrastructure.
items.summary: Review of the challenges, tradeoffs and new threats in building private and confidential AI inference infrastructure at production scale.

hl.t: Reviews the challenges and tradeoffs of building private inference infrastructure for AI at scale.
Draws on real production systems to report the performance impact of confidential inference.
Covers new threats specific to confidential inference that arise from how LLMs are operated.
Assesses whether providers can uphold privacy and confidentiality at a meaningful bar without unacceptable cost.

items.title: Agent Authorization Is Not a Vault Problem
items.abstract:
Almost every agent-approval product shows the human a summary produced by the thing being approved. The signature covers bytes, the human reads prose, and nothing binds the two.

We built the device that has to see, display and approve the exact bytes before a key signs: a real USB authenticator that gates ssh logins and FIDO2 assertions on a physical button. Then we attacked our own protocol before implementing it. Our first design had the desktop signing bytes chosen by the remote server, which is a signing oracle wearing a co-authorization costume. Our bring-up firmware answered plaintext control frames on an unprivileged HID channel.

The transferable finding: any co-authorization design that reaches for a detached signature over the operation has probably built the same oracle. All open source, MIT OR Apache-2.0.
items.summary: A hardware USB authenticator that gates agent actions by signing exact bytes, and the co-authorization oracle flaw it avoids.

hl.t: Presents a USB authenticator that displays and approves the exact bytes before a key signs an ssh login or FIDO2 assertion.
Shows how co-authorization over a detached signature becomes a signing oracle, using the team's own first design.
Argues most agent-approval products bind a signature to bytes while the human reads unbound prose.
Hardware and protocol released as open source under MIT or Apache-2.0.
Co-presented by a KonaSense CTO and a vulnerability researcher from Anthropic.

items.title: Everyone Wants All the AI Tools. Good.
items.abstract: At a fast-moving tech company, everyone wants every AI tool, by this afternoon. They should. These tools are incredibly powerful. The problem is that agents are designed to finish the task, not respect risk tolerance they were never given. This talk covers how to govern AI without defaulting to “no” or sending every use case through central review. Start by aligning leadership on risk and redlines. Turn that into self-service paved roads, secure agent sandboxes, technical guardrails, and detection or blocking for the paths outside your tolerance.
items.summary: A CISO approach to governing employee AI tool use through aligned redlines, paved roads, secure sandboxes and technical guardrails.

hl.t: Presents how to govern AI tool adoption without defaulting to no or routing every use case through central review.
The approach starts by aligning leadership on risk tolerance and redlines.
Turns redlines into self-service paved roads, secure agent sandboxes, and technical guardrails.
Adds detection and blocking for the paths that fall outside risk tolerance.

items.title: Coffee break
Enterprise OpenClaw: Tackling Agentic Security at Scale
items.abstract: Work inside a modern company rarely lives in one place, and while having an AI agent execute tasks across GitHub, Slack, and production systems sounds great, it is a security nightmare if not properly architected. This talk explores how Felix Pago built an identity-aware, secure agent runtime using OpenClaw to run AI workflows at scale. We will dive deep into the systems engineering required for secure AI tool use: separating Requester, Actor, and Persona via our explicit actAs model, eliminating long-lived credentials via ephemeral token minting, sandboxing with gVisor, and enforcing read-only guardrails. Move beyond prompt engineering and learn how to actually build and operate an audited, least-privilege agent fleet of over 500 pods in production.
items.summary: How Felix Pago built an identity-aware agent runtime with ephemeral tokens, gVisor sandboxing and guardrails across 500 production pods.

hl.t: Describes an identity-aware agent runtime built on OpenClaw running a fleet of over 500 pods in production.
Separates Requester, Actor, and Persona through an explicit actAs model.
Eliminates long-lived credentials with ephemeral token minting and sandboxes agents with gVisor.
Enforces read-only guardrails across an audited, least-privilege agent fleet.

items.title: Same Threat, Two Verdicts: Shadow Testing Our SOC Agent
items.abstract:
Our autonomous SOC agent has handled 5,000 threats a day for a year, yet the same threat could yield two well-supported but opposite verdicts. When a metric moved, was it the change or instability?

We split the end-to-end agent: an investigation agent writes structured findings; a verdict agent reads only them and decides. This did not eliminate nondeterminism but revealed whether instability came from evidence or judgment.

A/A test runs traced most variation to our playbooks, flat lists of 10–15 questions; the agent picked a different subset each run. Recipes replaced them: staged plans of mandatory and optional steps naming the evidence to seek and the tool to use.

With baseline variance measured and reduced, shadow tests became meaningful: a silent candidate runs on the same threats as production, scored on agreement, FPR and precision against analyst ground truth and expected noise.

Attendees learn to decompose, constrain, measure, and safely ship changes to production agents.
items.summary: How a production SOC agent was split and tested to measure nondeterminism and safely ship changes using recipes and shadow tests.

hl.t: Tackles nondeterminism in a SOC agent that has handled 5,000 threats a day for a year.
Splits the agent into an investigation agent that writes findings and a verdict agent that reads only them.

items.title: BITE – Behavior-Intent Traceable Evaluation
items.abstract:
Scanners for extensions, skills, and MCP servers hit a precision wall: too many false positives. We address this by mapping behavioral signals, connecting them into chains, and interpreting them against the program’s intent.

The flow:

1. Map signals such as credential reads, outbound calls, and file writes. Each can be legitimate on its own.

2. Connect signals into behavior chains.

3. Apply BITE (Behavior-Intent Traceable Evaluation): compare each chain with stated intent to decide whether it is legitimate, risky, or malicious.

BITE is the key innovation. Rather than use the model as a black-box classifier, We ground its judgment in evidence from the artifact: code, connected behaviors, internal structure, and declared purpose. This reduces false positives, cost, and inconsistent judgments while keeping verdicts traceable to evidence. Stricter intent checks may also create false negatives.

Using malicious cases, we show what failed, what improved, and where the approach falls short.
items.summary: A method that maps behavioral signals in extensions, skills and MCP servers into chains and judges them against stated intent.

hl.t: Introduces BITE, comparing an artifact's behavior chains against its stated intent to judge extensions, skills, and MCP servers.
Maps signals such as credential reads, outbound calls, and file writes, then connects them into behavior chains.
Grounds the model's verdict in evidence from code and declared purpose rather than black-box classification.
Reports reduced false positives alongside the false negatives that stricter intent checks can introduce.

items.title: Threat Model Impossible: 1 Agent. 30 Days. 687 Security Reviews. And a Refrigerator.
items.abstract:
We built an in-house threat model agent that completed 687 AI-assisted security reviews in 30 days, documented 3k+ risks in Jira, and routed remediation to system owners. Building the agent wasn’t the hardest part. It was getting reliable system and ownership data, then using deterministic automation to turn AI output into structured Jira risk tickets.

The pipeline starts with a 50-question owner survey. Copilot Studio reasons over the system artifacts. Power Automate validates the output and assigns the work. Humans then validate the results and escalate higher-risk systems into deeper threat model reviews using code, data-flow diagrams, and architecture documents.

I’ll show what we built, how we scaled it, what broke, and how the agent ended up threat modeling unexpected things like a refrigerator. I’ll close with our plan to embed reviews into application platforms so they kick off as soon as systems are onboarded.

Hacking Truth: Forged Lean Proofs and the Risk of Verifier Bugs
items.abstract:
Bugs in provers like Lean and Rocq can let you prove 1=0 and other falsehoods. That’s nothing new. But in the age of “vericoding” the stakes have changed. How much trust should we place in machine-checked proofs and formally verified cryptographic software? We revisit seven previously reported soundness bugs in Lean and Rocq, some still unpatched. Recognizing them as security vulnerabilities, we requested and obtained seven CVEs. Exploiting these bugs, we show:

– Forged proofs of P = NP, the Riemann Hypothesis, and other Millennium Prize Problems. Our proofs are deliberately short and unlikely to fool an expert human reviewer, but more elaborate and convincing forgeries could be constructed.

– A sabotaged Fiat-Crypto field multiplier that always returns zero, while its original correctness theorem remains accepted. Fiat-Crypto-derived code is used by BoringSSL and other prominent projects.

– We also demonstrate soundness failures in Z3, including one that makes downstream verification tools accept false claims.

We provide reproducible Docker PoCs for these results. None of the prover/verifier projects appeared to have a documented security disclosure policy. It’s now time to treat them as security boundaries and prioritize fixing exploitable bugs, with proper disclosure processes, lest more false proofs and results creep into the ecosystem, accidentally or maliciously. Finally, we present a new 1911-line Rocq formalization of a constructive reduction to Rice’s theorem, concerning the undecidability of nontrivial semantic properties of programs, which got us started on this research.
items.summary: Seven soundness bugs in Lean, Rocq and Z3 that forge proofs and sabotage verified cryptographic code, with reproducible proof of concept.

hl.t: Revisits seven soundness bugs in the Lean and Rocq proof assistants and obtains seven CVEs for them.
Forges short proofs of P=NP, the Riemann Hypothesis, and other Millennium Prize Problems.

items.title: Beyond the SBOM: Proving Process Integrity with the Open PBOM Specification

speakers.a: Cybersecurity Engineer, Application Security Architect, Visa

items.abstract:
Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) standards answer one vital question:

What binaries and open-source libraries are packed into this artifact? However, modern supply chain attacks—from compromise of CI runners to poisoned build dependencies—target the assembly mechanism itself. Knowing what is inside a container does not tell you how it was built, who approved the pipeline execution, or whether the build environment was tampered with in transit.

To solve this, we released the open Pipeline Bill of Materials (PBOM) Specification on GitHub. The PBOM specification establishes a standardized, machine-readable schema for capturing the complete execution context of a build pipeline—including runner identities, environment configurations, git lineage, active policy evaluations, and cryptographic signatures at every stage.
items.summary: An open Pipeline Bill of Materials specification that captures build pipeline execution context to prove process integrity beyond the SBOM.

hl.t: Introduces the open Pipeline Bill of Materials (PBOM) specification for capturing a build pipeline's execution context.
The PBOM schema records runner identities, environment configs, git lineage, policy evaluations, and signatures at every stage.
Targets supply chain attacks on the assembly mechanism itself, such as CI runner compromise and poisoned build dependencies.
Released on GitHub by security engineers from Visa and Cigna.

items.title: Coffee break
Twelve Consoles, One Investigation
items.abstract: Security teams do not lack tools they lack the connective layer between them. Answering a simple question like “is this login legitimate?” often requires hopping across a dozen siloed consoles, manually pasting context, and performing cross system correlation entirely in an analyst’s head. To eliminate this bottleneck, we paired an ex-law enforcement investigator with a security engineer to build an automated, agentic investigation system. By routing queries dynamically across enterprise integrations, the system exposes hidden, multi-system threats, such as a localized login hiding an impossibly high network latency, or a Latveria RF signature on a device reporting an American IP. Attendees will walk away with practical, production-tested blueprints: a GET-pinned read-only driver pattern, indicator-based routing logic, and a permission model designed for safe, unattended operation.
items.summary: An agentic investigation system at Oscar Health that routes queries across siloed consoles to expose hidden multi-system threats.

hl.t: Presents an agentic investigation system that routes queries across a dozen enterprise consoles to answer questions like whether a login is legitimate.
Surfaces hidden multi-system threats by correlating signals across otherwise siloed tools.
Built by pairing an ex-law-enforcement investigator with a security engineer.

We don’t need an LLM for That
items.abstract:
Zero-shot LLMs are easy to deploy, therefore stakeholders ask why fund classical ML. We test this assumption using zero-shot frontier LLMs, XGBoost, fine-tuning, and two LLM-ML ensembles, on phishing and network attack detection. Three network datasets come from one Mirai capture rebuilt at three aggregation levels, isolating representation as the variable.

The answer is nuanced. On phishing, zero-shot LLMs hit 0.970 AUCPR, but a fine-tuned encoder beats them at 0.998. On network traffic, zero-shot LLMs are guessing “attack” almost every time, with one narrow exception that still trails XGBoost. XGBoost stays strong, and routing uncertain cases to the LLM makes results worse. A high class prior or a leaky split can each fake an “LLMs work” result, a trap fine-tuning or evaluation on network data hits.

We bring fine-tuning runs, AUCPR-vs-class-prior numbers across four representations, and a decision guide: which model, which representation, per task and budget.
items.summary: Empirical comparison of zero-shot LLMs, XGBoost and fine-tuning on phishing and network attack detection, with a model selection guide.

items.title: Lunch break
Approval Is Not Human Presence: Building and Breaking an MCP Permission Broker

speakers.a: Security Engineer & AI Security Researcher, Dropbox

items.abstract:
An AI agent on a developer workstation often inherits the same UID, groups, environment, and credentials as its human operator. In that setting, an “Approve” action is just input the agent may be able to generate and not necessarily evidence that a human participated.

This talk presents a deployed MCP permission broker that requires evidence of human presence before granting sensitive capabilities as well as allowing for different coding agent sessions running as the same user to have different permissions. I’ll reconstruct a live boundary test run from the strongest position the agent held: the human’s UID, membership in the admin group, a writable source checkout, and a valid broker session.

Attendees will leave with a practical threat model, enforcement pattern, and adversarial test plan for making human approval a real security boundary.
items.summary: A deployed MCP permission broker that requires evidence of human presence before sensitive actions, with an adversarial test plan.

hl.t: Presents a deployed MCP permission broker that requires evidence of human presence before granting sensitive capabilities.
Argues an Approve click is just input an agent sharing the user's UID may be able to generate.
Reconstructs a live boundary test from the strongest position the agent held, including admin-group membership and a valid broker session.
Lets different coding-agent sessions running as the same user hold different permissions.

items.title: Reading the Residual Stream: Productizing Activation-Probe Security at Intuit

speakers.a: AI Security & Safety Architect | GenAI Security, Threat Modeling, and AI-Assisted Risk Assessment, Intuit

items.abstract: Production guardrails come in two flavors: LLM judges — a full autoregressive pass per check, and a judge that can itself be prompt-injected — and trained text classifiers: cheap, but blind to paraphrase, obfuscation, and image-borne attacks. This talk makes the case for a third path: generation-free guardrails. One forward pass through a small (2–4B) open-weight model, read its internal activations, classify them with lightweight probes — no tokens generated, no prompt to inject into, and the signal is what the model understood, not what the text says. We show how to build one: which signals to read, training probes with modest labeled data, and the engineering that makes it production-grade — activation extraction with early exit, cross-request GPU batching (~4.1s to under 820ms, bit-exact), calibration at sub-0.1% FPR. We compare against open detectors and frontier judges on 20+ public datasets, and share what broke on the way to production at a large fintech.
items.summary: Generation-free guardrails at Intuit that read a small model's activations with lightweight probes to detect attacks without generating tokens.

hl.t: Makes the case for generation-free guardrails that read a small model's internal activations instead of generating tokens.
Uses one forward pass through a 2 to 4B open-weight model and classifies the activations with lightweight probes.
Reports engineering that cut latency from about 4.1 seconds to under 820 milliseconds, bit-exact, at sub-0.1% false-positive rate.

items.title: Engineering Context for SOC Agents: Lessons, Failures, and Open Questions

speakers.a: Cloud Security AI Engineer, Google Cloud Security

items.abstract:
I started building SOC AI workflows with a simple setup: Markdown AI runbooks (what we now call Agent Skills) piped into a local Cline harness, and it worked surprisingly well. Moving to an enterprise agent platform opened an embarrassment of riches, but created a whole new set of engineering dilemmas that I am still figuring out.

I now have persistent investigation memory for free, but how do I pick which memories are relevant? I can ground SIEM telemetry with the entirety of enterprise context, but what context should I actually inject? Given Model Garden, how do I decide which model to use?

This talk is not corporate shilling for Google’s agent platform; it is an honest inquiry from a software builder and architect in the trenches. I will share what I’ve tried, what broke, the problems I’ve seen and heard, the trade-offs I am wrestling with, and open questions. I would love to compare notes with the audience.
items.summary: An honest account of context engineering for SOC agents, covering memory selection, context injection, model choice and open questions.

hl.t: Shares lessons from building SOC AI workflows, from Markdown runbooks in a local Cline harness to an enterprise agent platform.
Examines which stored memories are relevant and what enterprise context to inject when grounding SIEM telemetry.
Works through the trade-off of choosing which model to use for SOC investigation.
Framed as an honest inquiry into open questions rather than a platform pitch.

items.title: Building Security Review Agents: the Models are the Reliable Part
items.abstract:
Employees connect third-party and custom apps to Google Workspace and Slack [and more] faster than a small security team can review them. This is not an AppSec review: there is no author to interview and no build to block, just a client ID and a list of permissions describing access someone is already using. We built a review pipeline where several models assess each grant independently, a stronger model referees when they disagree, and a human decides. We wrapped that non-deterministic core in deterministic guardrails, which is exactly what you are supposed to do.

Then we audited it. The verdict we stored disagreed with the reasoning we showed the reviewer. A model quietly stopped counting toward the score. A service ran clean for twelve days and produced nothing. Almost nothing that went wrong was the model. This talk is what we found, what we fixed, and why a human is still in the loop.
items.summary: A multi-model pipeline at Twilio that reviews third-party app access grants, and the audit that found the failures were not the models.

hl.t: Describes a pipeline where several models independently assess each app permission grant and a stronger model referees disagreements.
Reviews third-party and custom app grants to Google Workspace and Slack, access that is already in use.
Audit found the stored verdict disagreed with the reasoning shown, and a model quietly stopped counting toward the score.

items.title: Coffee break
From Patch Generation to Evidence: Building Trust in AI-Generated Code
items.abstract:
AI can generate patches faster than humans can review them. The next challenge is deciding whether these patches deserve our trust.

This talk shares the engineering lessons that shaped the OpenAnt Auto Patcher trust architecture: which forms of evidence proved useful, which intuitive ideas failed to improve quality, and how controlled experiments refined the boundary between LLM reasoning and deterministic policy.

This session focuses on designing systems that make, and communicate, trustworthy decisions.

Beyond sufficient regression tests, flow analysis, and other known techniques, using agents, we can build trust in the system and the patches generated.

For example, are patches for past vulnerabilities, generated by Auto Patcher, semantically equivalent to patches previously generated by maintainers? Then, how do we train our system based on that?

Attendees will leave with practical principles for designing autonomous patching systems and, by extension, AI-assisted systems.
items.summary: Engineering lessons on building a trust architecture for AI-generated patches, using evidence and experiments to decide which fixes to trust.

hl.t: Shares the trust architecture behind the OpenAnt Auto Patcher for AI-generated security patches.
Reports which forms of evidence improved patch quality and which intuitive ideas failed.
Tests whether generated patches are semantically equivalent to patches maintainers produced for past vulnerabilities.
Refines the boundary between LLM reasoning and deterministic policy through controlled experiments.

items.title: When Humans Can’t Make It Hard Enough: Self-Hardening Environments for Frontier AI Investigators
items.abstract:
Attacks are going out of distribution. Hiding tracks, tampering with logs, even AI-driven zero-days: in a real 2026 incident, AI agents faked their own tool calls and tried (and failed) to delete their logs. Our tests can’t keep up: hard cyber evals and public benchmarks like Splunk’s BOTS are saturating.

Training a good investigator already works, once it can practice in realistic environments. For SOC investigation those barely exist, so the scarce thing is building them at scale. We call this env-play: a generator improving its scenarios against a fixed investigator, hunting the hardest still-solvable cases. Every scenario is judged on three dimensions: realism, solvability, and difficulty.

We’ll show what broke GPT-5.6-Sol (right verdict in ~8% of runs), what didn’t (noise, scripted tricks), and why we read its queries, not its score, in a live demo. You’ll leave with a loop for testing whether your agent can investigate or has merely learned your benchmark.
items.summary: An env-play loop that generates realistic SOC scenarios to stress-test AI investigators as benchmarks saturate, shown in a live demo.

hl.t: Introduces env-play, a generator that produces SOC investigation scenarios against a fixed investigator, hunting the hardest still-solvable cases.
Scores every generated scenario on realism, solvability, and difficulty.
Reports a generated environment where GPT-5.6-Sol reached the right verdict in about 8% of runs.
Includes a live demo reading the investigator's queries rather than its score.
Motivated by saturating public benchmarks like Splunk's BOTS and a 2026 incident where agents faked tool calls.

items.title: When Evaluation Runs Start Talking to Each Other
items.abstract:
Agents assigned separate evaluation tasks can discover one another through shared infrastructure or public internet services, exchange answers and techniques, and build on work that persists across runs. These interactions can turn supposedly independent attempts into a system with shared memory and pooled effort, changing what the scores measure.

Drawing on our work building and evaluating cyber agents, we examine how supporting infrastructure can become an alternative path to success, undermining evaluation validity and enabling unauthorized actions. During reinforcement learning, rewarding these shortcuts can also reinforce behavior the training process was meant to avoid.

We examine why isolating execution alone does not establish independence, and how to preserve realistic tools and connectivity while protecting grading integrity and enforcing authorization boundaries.
items.summary: How agents in separate evaluation runs discover each other through shared infrastructure, pooling effort and undermining evaluation validity.

hl.t: Shows how agents on separate evaluation tasks discover each other through shared infrastructure and pool answers and effort.
Explains how such interactions turn supposedly independent attempts into a system with shared memory, changing what scores measure.
Argues that isolating execution alone does not establish independence between evaluation runs.
Warns that rewarding these shortcuts during reinforcement learning reinforces the behavior training was meant to avoid.

**Description:**

Pointing a model at a repository and asking it to “find all the vulnerabilities” is not vulnerability research and is overwhelming software maintainters with poor quality reports. The same models can produce radically different results depending on the context, tools, constraints, and methodology wrapped around it.

In this hands-on workshop, participants will select a real open-source project and build a bespoke security research harness for it. Using Claude Code or Codex as a baseline, we will improve the agent’s capabilities by learning and implementing harness engineering techniques to improve finding quality.

Participants will build their harness to identify vulnerabilities by mapping attack surfaces, inspecting source code, and validating potentially vulnerable behavior by running software dynamically.

Participants will leave with a working research harness and a reusable methodology for how to tune it to find, validate, and disclose findings. No prior harness-engineering experience is required. This is for people who have used mainstream agents for security purposes but want to move beyond one-off prompts.

**Prerequisites:**

- Have used a mainstream coding agent such as Codex, Claude Code, or an equivalent tool.
- Be comfortable using a terminal, Git, and a source repository.
- Be able to read source code in at least one programming language.
- Understand basic vulnerability research concepts

Administrator access to install and run development tools.

workshops.details:
**Description:**

A SOC drowns in what we send it. Every team forwards every log line and every finding, most of them marked high, and the analysts are left to sort it out. The teams that own the systems know best what matters, so that is where the sorting should start.

In this workshop you build a ranking layer for a small application. Nothing gets dropped. Every log line is still stored, but your layer decides what deserves the SOC’s attention. You work with the application’s logs and its misconfigurations, and one real attack is hidden among a lot of harmless noise. You rank what you find with simple scoring and an LLM, and you link incidents to the misconfigurations that make them dangerous. Then you check if the attack lands at the top of the analyst’s queue.
A ranker that reads logs can be fooled by whoever writes them. In the last part you attack your own pipeline with a log line built to bury the attack, and then you fix it.

workshops.title: Finding Vulnerabilities with AgentGG AI Agents: A Hands-On Workshop
workshops.details:
**Description:**

AgentGG CLI is an open-source tool that uses AI agents to find, validate and score security vulnerabilities in source code. We’ve used it to find 40+ zero-days that were accepted by open-source projects, including a critical SQL injection in GeoServer (CVE-2026-76904, CVSS 9.8). In this workshop, we share what we learned about reducing false positives and keeping scan costs down.

Participants run AgentGG against a deliberately vulnerable app and triage the results. We walk through each stage of a scan, from recon to validation and CVSS scoring. Participants then write their own detection agent, which consists of a precondition, a seeding strategy using regex or Semgrep, and a prompt written in markdown. They tune the agent to reduce false positives and add it to a CI pipeline that scans pull requests. By the end, participants will have a working custom agent and a CI workflow they can use on their own code. No prior experience building AI agents is required.

**Prerequisites:**

Basic terminal and git skills, the ability to read code, and familiarity with common web vulnerabilities like SQL injection and XSS.

**Participant Setup Requirements:**

A laptop with Node.js, git, and a GitHub account.

**Description:**

This 2-hour hands-on workshop uses a sandboxed assistant to show how persistent memory and file tools create an attack path between users. Assistants with persistent memory and file tools are becoming the default way people work with agents, and they share files with each other all the time. We will build a small assistant with a memory store, file read and write tools, and a shared folder. workshops.title: Reinforcement Learning for Open-Weight Security LLMs, with a Live Training Run

speakers.a: Principal AI Researcher, Averlon | Training LLMs for Cybersecurity

workshops.details:
**Description:**

In our benchmarks, open-weight LLMs match closed models on most security tasks at far lower cost, and reinforcement learning (RL) makes them task experts. This hands-on workshop teaches RL through security examples: vulnerability discovery, penetration testing and detection engineering. An LLM judge, serving as the reward model, accepts or rejects samples; accepted ones join a growing training pool. If most are rejected, iterative self-refinement improves them; failing that, a stronger open model or human annotations seed the pool. Verifiers are slower, so each round trains on judge-accepted samples, but only verified samples stay in the pool, since judges can be gamed. Adapting sampling and the reward model keeps training stable. In our experiments, many complicated RL methods proved unnecessary, and some failed outright.

The live case study targets over-refusal: safety-tuned LLMs sometimes decline authorized penetration testing. Abliteration, which strips refusal from the weights, is a poor fix: in our tests it was unreliable on reasoning models and hurt capability, and it disarms refusals for attackers too. Instead, RL retrains Gemma 4 12B live to help with authorized work while still refusing harmful requests. Participants red-team each checkpoint as a dashboard tracks false refusals and harmful compliance.

**Prerequisites:**

- A coding agent such as Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode; our skill files let it build and run the labs.
- No machine-learning, RL or model-training experience needed.
- Helpful: penetration-testing or other security experience. ML practitioners new to security are equally welcome.

**Participant Setup Requirements:**

- A laptop with a coding agent such as Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode. No GPU needed.
- Lab files and endpoint access, sent in advance with a short setup check.

workshops.details:
**Description:**

The scanner found a real vulnerability. Engineering needs to know where to change the code, whether the fix will break anything, and how to get it into customers’ hands. Meanwhile, security has another hundred findings to work through.

This workshop follows one issue through that process. Starting with a sample application and a mixed queue of findings, we’ll decide what needs attention, identify the affected code and configuration, and use a coding agent to propose a fix. We’ll inspect the patch, test it, and work through what happens when it fails. We’ll also cover the EU Cyber Resilience Act: when a finding needs to be reported, who owns that decision, and why a reporting deadline is different from a patch deadline. The exercise ends with a release decision and a record of what was fixed, what was tested, and what remains exposed. No Mythos access is needed.

workshops.details:
**Description:**

The world of AI hype cycles is typically dominated by the latest generative AI trends: new chatbots, image and video generators, coding agents, and synthetic music. But just a few weeks ago, Diogo Almeida, a co-creator of ChatGPT, launched a new model series called Jev that doesn’t generate text or images. Instead, it makes fast, probabilistic decisions over defined choices, producing answers that software can act on directly, igniting a renewed interest in the many other forms of AI that most have not been exposed to.

This workshop will focus on the others. The non-generative AI world. We will explore purpose-built tiny models, general models adapted to domain-specific tasks, classifiers, embedding and similarity models, reinforcement learning systems, the emerging class of Jev-like decision models, and yes, even a synthetic reconstruction of a fly’s neurological connectome playing games and driving decisions and outcomes.

Over the course of two hours we will learn about model training, classifiers, reinforcement learning, and how to apply what seems like fun and games to navigating workflows and desision trees in arbitrary business logic and even extending the ability of more generalized LLM agents with new super powers.

Join us as we explore the fascinating world of non-generative AI, the unspoken, scalable powerhouse of AI that has been silently driving businesses processes globally for decades.

workshops.details:
**Description:**

AI coding assistants collapse the time between “I need a tool for this” and having one running, but only if you use them well. Asking a model for a whole application at once reliably produces hallucinated APIs, incoherent architecture, and code you don’t understand well enough to trust. This hands-on workshop teaches a “think then act” methodology for AI-assisted security tool development, using a custom payload evasion framework as the vehicle. Attendees prompt an assistant to produce a Product Requirements Document, review and correct that design against authoritative references, then implement in small, verifiable phases. The result is a containerized web application that accepts raw shellcode and emits C# loaders with configurable evasion options (payload bloating, sleep delays, anti-sandbox checks, environmental keying, domain-joined validation, entropy reduction), mapping to ATT&CK T1027, T1497.001, T1480.001, and T1055. The emphasis throughout is verification over generation.

None

workshops.title: Possession Is Not Permission: Hands-On Authority Control for Capable Agents

speakers.a: Head of AI Engineering, Mirror Security
Head of Partnership and Operations, Mirror Security

workshops.details:
**Description:**

Agents are getting better at finding another route. In July 2026, about 700 benchmark agents coordinated through a shared package registry, recovered credentials and crossed into a real third-party service. Nobody jailbroke them. The tasks were impossible, the goal stayed active, and every system on the path accepted a working credential as permission.

This workshop teaches one control that holds when the model, sandbox and monitor all miss: the system that commits a consequence verifies the original authority, not just a valid token. You start with a small agent harness and a mock destination that trusts bearer tokens. You break it with five attacks drawn from real incidents: goal substitution, credential retargeting, threshold splitting, delegation expansion and a compaction summary claiming approval. Then you build the check that stops them: a signed root goal, delegation that can only narrow, an exact action digest, a short-lived lease and a receipt tied to the destination’s real state. The approved work keeps running. The expanded action does not.

The kit is vendor-neutral Python built on familiar primitives (Macaroons, HTTP Message Signatures, Cedar-style policy). You leave with the repo, a worksheet and a checklist to apply to your own agents on Monday.

**Prerequisites:**

- Comfort reading and editing Python.
- Basic familiarity with HTTP APIs and what a bearer token is.
- No prior agent-security or cryptography background needed: the kit supplies the signing and policy primitives and every step is guided by a test.

**Participant Setup Requirements:**

- A laptop with Python 3.11+ (or Docker Desktop), git and a terminal.
- Before the session: clone the repository from the link we send out and run the one-line setup so dependencies are cached; a USB copy may be available in the room.

workshops.title: Zero Trust for the Agentic SOC: Building, Governing, and Stress-Testing in the AI Era [SANS]

speakers.a: SANS Author and Senior Instructor, VP of Labs, Threat Research and Intelligence at Arctic Wolf

workshops.details:
**Description:**

An attacker phishes an OAuth consent grant, steals a Primary Refresh Token, and quietly maps partner tenants: no password cracked, no signature tripped. Detecting it is the easy part; the real question is what happens in the minutes after. Attendees sit inside an agentic incident-response pipeline as its architect, its governor, and finally its stress-tester. After a short briefing reconstructing a Silk Typhoon-style intrusion, they go hands-on with a working LangGraph workflow: normalizing raw Entra ID logs into OCSF, tracing an agent that correlates signals across identity, network, endpoint, and data layers, computing a composite risk score, and receiving a live LLM-recommended containment action. At the Human-in-the-Loop gate, each attendee must approve, override, or escalate the AI’s decision with documented justification before enforcement fires through a Policy Decision Point to Policy Enforcement Point chain against a Conditional Access API. Then they stress-test their own pipeline the way an adversary would: first holding the composite risk score just below the enforcement threshold while the intrusion proceeds, then turning the agent’s over-privileged credentials against it to tamper with the detection dataset and watch the risk score collapse.

**Prerequisites:**

workshops.title: Your Agent’s Approval Prompt Is an Attack Surface. Gate It.
workshops.details:
**Description:**

Human-in-the-loop is the control everyone cites for agent safety, and in practice it is a person pressing 1. Claude Code users approve 93% of permission prompts. OWASP’s Agentic Top 10 calls the result ASI09, human-agent trust exploitation: a fluent agent, a tired reviewer, and a malicious action waved through. Slopsquatted packages, a secrets file swept into a commit, a shell command built from user input, an instruction planted in a ticket: each passes the same prompt.

SP1 Gate is an open-source control for that step. It hooks into Claude Code and holds a risky action until the human answers factual questions about what it will do, with answer keys computed deterministically from the parsed command and the code’s syntax tree, out of band from the model. A compromised agent cannot answer its own quiz.

In two hours, you will install the gate, drive six attack-shaped prompts through it, write and test a detection rule for a command it currently misses, then red-team it: as the agent, try to get a risky action past the gate, and file what works. We close by measuring the control itself, hit rate against seeded malicious proposals versus false alarms, so you can say what it caught.

**Prerequisites:**

- Comfortable in a terminal
- basic Python (you can read a function and write an if statement)
- have used an AI coding agent at least once.

**Participant Setup Requirements:**

Before arriving:

- Laptop with Python 3.9 or later (macOS and Linux tested Windows users should use WSL).
- Claude Code installed and signed in (Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise or Console account); confirm Claude starts before you arrive.
- git and a clone of github.com/ritasabri/sp1-gate
- A browser that can open pages served from 127.0.0.1.

workshops.title: Benign Until It Isn’t: Build a Sleeper Skill, Then Catch It
workshops.details:
**Description:**

Your team is already installing agent skills, or is about to, and the review step most people rely on returns a verdict that does not mean what it sounds like. A skill can pass scanning and human review, then reach files, tools, and identity surfaces its description never mentions. Or it can behave one way under review and another way once it ships.

This workshop teaches you to catch both by making you build them first. In a contained sandbox, you audit a skill that already carries a benign verdict and map what it can actually reach, dependency chain and identity-file writes included. Then you build a sleeper skill yourself, watch it pass the gate, and watch it wake up, so the detection signal is something you have seen rather than read about. The second half is defense. You run static, dependency-graph, and behavioral runtime detection across a mixed set of skills, score where each layer catches and misses, then write an acceptance checklist and runtime guardrails and test them against your own sleeper. The target is containment that does not lobotomize the agent. You leave with the checklist, the guardrails, and the sandbox.

**Prerequisites:**

- Comfort reading code and configuration, mostly Python and JSON-style files, and basic command-line or browser-IDE use.
-  No AI or machine-learning background is required and no prior experience with agent skills is assumed; the session defines what it needs as it goes.
- If you have ever reviewed a dependency or written a detection rule, you are over-qualified for the entry bar and will get plenty out of the later modules.

**Participant Setup Requirements:**

- A laptop with a modern browser and nothing installed.
- Lab accounts are pre-issued on site, so there is no signup, no personal email login, and no admin rights needed.
- If you prefer to work locally instead of in the hosted sandbox, install Docker and clone the workshop repository beforehand; the repo link will arrive roughly one week ahead. Either path works and you can switch mid-session.
